APPEALS BOARD.-The Department of Commerce Appeals Board is an impartial body empowered to consider and decide appeals from administrative action in the areas of export controls, allocations of domestic materials and products, and the importation of foreign excess property under authorities vested in or delegated to the Sec retary of Commerce by law. The 

Board similarly disposes of appeals from other administrative actions, such as contract appeals, taken pursuant to law and referred to the Board by appropriate authority.

Area Redevelopment Administration 

 Regu lations, Title 13, Chapter III] CREATION AND AUTHORITY.—The Area Redevelopment Administration was established by the Secretary of

Commerce, by Department Order 171 

of May 8, 1961, pursuant to authority vested in the Secretary of Commerce by the Area Redevelopment Act (75) 

Stat. 47; 42 U.S.C. 2501) and Reor ganization Plan 5 of 1950. Following enactment of the Public Works Accel eration Act (76 Stat. 541; 42 U.S.C. 

2641) and the issuance of Executive

Order 11049, Department Order 171 was amended on September 14, 1962, to establish within the Area Redevelopment Administration the Office of Pub lic Works Acceleration. 

PURPOSE. The primary function assigned the Area Redevelopment Ad ministration by statute is the economic redevelopment of areas of substantial and persistent unemployment and underemployment through the creation of new employment opportunities by developing new and expanding existing facilities and resources in such areas. 

ORGANIZATION. The organization of the Area Redevelopment Administra tion comprises the Office of the 

Administrator, the Office of Adminis tration and Finance, the Office of

Operations, the Office of Planning and 

Research, and the Office of Public Works Acceleration, at the Washing ton, D.C., headquarters.

Public Advisory Committee on Area 

Redevelopment serves to promote full exchange of views between the Government and the public, and an Area 

Redevelopment Advisory Policy Board 

(an interagency committee) helps assure coordinated action by Federal

Government agencies on area redevelopment matters. 

Field representatives of the Agency are located throughout the United

States and Puerto Rico. 

FUNCTIONS AND ACTIVITIES.-The 

Area Redevelopment Act authorizes certain Federal aids for areas designated by the Administrator as “redevelopment areas." These include loans for industrial or commercial facilities, loans and/or grants for public facilities, technical assistance, and related infor mation. The Area Redevelopment Ad ministration exercises program control and provides policy direction in furnishing such aid in close collaboration with other Federal agencies.

Under provisions of the Public Works Acceleration Act, the Adminis trator, in order to increase employment opportunities, prepares for the Secretary of Commerce recommendations on public works to be initiated and/or accelerated in "redevelopment areas" or in those areas designated as eligible for assistance under the Public Works 

Acceleration Act by the Secretary of 

Labor.

The Administration coordinates op- 

In accordance with the terms of the Area Redevelopment Act, a National erating functions under the Area Re-

development Act delegated by the 

Secretary of Commerce to the Departments of Agriculture, Health, Education, and Welfare, Interior, and Labor, to the Housing and Home Finance 

Agency, and to the Small Business Administration. These functions include technical assistance and economic development information as well as the processing of loan and grant applications.

The Administration's staff of field representatives provides direct assistance to State and local agencies concerned with, and engaged in, economic development activities.

Business and Defense Services Administration 

 Reg ulations, Title 15, Chapter VI; Title 32A, Chapter VI; Title 44, Chapter IV]  Business and Defense Services Admin istration was established by the Secretary of Commerce on October 1, 1953, by Department Order 152, pursuant to authority of Reorganization Plan 5 of 

1950. 

ORGANIZATION.-BDSA is headed by an Administrator who reports and is responsible to the Assistant Secretary for Domestic and International Business. Programs are carried out by 24 industry divisions, grouped by related industries in seven Offices: Distribution Services, Chemicals and Consumer 

Products, Industrial Equipment, Met als and Minerals, Scientific and Tech nical Equipment, Construction and Materials Industries, and Textiles. 

FUNCTIONS.-Staffed by profession als largely with previous business experience, BDSA collects, analyzes, and disseminates information of interest to business. BDSA's industrial and business analysts and economists, by anticipating broad changes in the business i climate, identifying their causes, and proposing remedial or adaptive action in conjunction with business, are frequently able to moderate the impact of such changes. By promoting renewal of antiquated plant, equipment, and management methods, and by advancing better methods of distribution and

Bl Tre S uctic TE marketing, BDSA assists in strengthening the competitive posture of U.S. industry at home and abroad. BDSA's collection of information on conditions in overseas industries is used by business to strengthen its distribution in the world market.

By presenting industry's views to other agencies of Government, BDSA assists in the formulation of policies which strengthen the economy as a whole.

BDSA's Industrial Analysis program identifies the causes of growth or retardation of industries, the impact of import competition on domestic businesses, and attempts to find solutions of maximum benefit to the business community.

INDUSTRIAL MOBILIZATION.- -BDSA 

also administers the authority delegated to the Secretary of Commerce under the Defense Production Act of 

1950, as amended, with respect to the use of priorities and directives that are necessary to support and expedite the accomplishment of current military, atomic energy, and space programs through the operation of the Defense

Materials System. It plans for industrial mobilization and production control in an emergency; conducts intensive training of a large contingent of the National Defense Executive Re serve; and provides advice and counsel to the Office of Emergency Planning on national stockpile operations.

TRADE ADJUSTMENT ASSISTANCE.- The Office of Trade Adjustment in 

BDSA is responsible for the administration of the program of trade adjustment for firms authorized under title 

III of the Trade Expansion Act of 

1962. Financial, technical, and tax assistance is authorized for eligible firms seriously injured by increased imports resulting from concessions granted in trade agreements. 

Office of Business Economics 

(1832 M Street NW., Washington, D.C., 20230)  Reg ulations, Title 15, Chapter VIII] The Office of Business Economics provides basic economic measures of the national economy, current analysis of the economic situation and business outlook, the United States balance of international payments, measurement and analysis of the factors affecting regional economic development in the 

United States, and general economic research on the functioning of the economy. For its analyses the Office develops economic and statistical indicators, and its national income and product work provides a basis for policy formulation by the Department, other executive agencies, and the Congress, with respect to Government operations insofar as they affect economic movements. Its services to business are long established and well known through the official monthly journal 

Survey of Current Business. The Office of Business Economics organi zation includes six major operating units: National Income Division, Regional Economics Division, National Economics Division, Current Business Analysis Division, Business Structure Division, and the Balance of Payments Division. 

Bureau of the Census (Suitland, Md., 20235. Phone, 735-2000) [For regulations codified under this heading, see Code of Federal Reg ulations, Title 15, Chapter I]  lished by the Constitution, which profunction of census taking was estab- vides that an enumeration of the peo-

ple shall be taken every 10 years in the manner in which the Congress shall direct. The act of March 6, 1902 (32

Stat. 51), established the Census Of fice as a permanent bureau. The act of 

February 14, 1903, transferred the

Census Office to the Department of 

Commerce and Labor. Laws pertain ing to the Bureau of the Census were codified as title 13, United States

Code. 

PURPOSE.- -Census taking was established for the primary purpose of apportioning Representatives and direct taxes among the States on the basis of population. A population census has been taken decennially since 

1790. Other subjects have regularly been included as needs arose and statistical projects were assigned to the Bureau. 

ORGANIZATION.-In addition to the headquarters at Suitland, Md., the

Bureau maintains a Census Opera tions Office at Jeffersonville, Ind., a

Personal Census Service Branch at 

Pittsburg, Kans., and 12 field organization offices.

FUNCTIONS AND ACTIVITIES.-The 

Bureau is responsible for conducting periodic censuses, sample surveys, and other current data collections, and furnishing statistical services to other

Government agencies. 

MAJOR CENSUSES.-The schedule of major censuses regularly taken is: population and housing, years ending in 0; agriculture, years ending in 4 and 9; drainage and irrigation, years ending in 9; governments, years ending in 2 and 7; and manufactures, mineral industries, business, and transportation, years ending in 3 and 8. 

CURRENT PROGRAMS.Data col lected at monthly, quarterly, or annual intervals provide up-to-date information on many subjects covered in the major censuses, on construction, and on U.S. foreign trade. 

POPULATION. The number, loca tion, and personal and family characteristics of the population, such as age, sex, race, marital status, place of birth, mother tongue of the foreign born, work status, occupation, education, mobility, and income, are included in the decennial census. The sample survey of the population provides current estimates of personal and family characteristics, population mobility, school enrollment, educational attainment, number and characteristics of households, income, and consumer buying indicators.

Monthly estimates of the total population and annual estimates by age, color, and sex are made; annual estimates for States are prepared; and projections of the population are furnished periodically. 

Special censuses in local areas are taken at the request and expense of the local governments. 

HOUSING.- -Statistics on the number and characteristics of housing units, such as number of rooms, persons per room, year built, tenure, value or rent, vacancy status, water supply, facilities, and equipment are provided by the decennial census of housing. Current housing statistics include data on rates, condition, and characteristics of housing vacancies, by geographic region. 

AGRICULTURE.-The agriculture cen sus provides data on the production and sale of farm products; farm and operator characteristics; farm labor, equipment, and facilities; cost of major farm inputs; use of agricultural chemicals; and farm values. The censuses of drainage and irrigation provide information on the number, characteristics, and extent of irrigation and drainage enterprises. 

Statistics on cotton ginnings by State and county are published periodically during each season; detailed statistics on cotton production and distribution are published annually.

INDUSTRY.-The census of manufac tures provides data on employment, payrolls, materials consumption, shipments, value added by manufacture, AAA I LIVIER

inventories, capital expenditures, and gross book value of fixed assets and rent - payments. R&B e pr The Bureau conducts an annual survey of manufactures for intercensal years and a comprehensive monthly survey of manufacturers' shipments, inventories, and orders. It also issues. about 100 series of monthly, quarterly, and annual reports on the current output, shipments, and stocks of the more important manufactured products.

The census of mineral industries provides measures of activity in the mining of coal, iron, and other metals and minerals, and the extraction of oil and gas including employment, payrolls, and value added in mining.

As a part of the 1963 economic census program, a census of commercial fisheries is being taken to provide measures of employment, payrolls, vessels, gear, and value of catch.

BUSINESS. The census of business, covering retail and wholesale trade and selected services, provides data on number of establishments, sales, employment, and payroll, by kind of business; and on subjects such as employment size, sales or receipts size, and legal form of organization. It also provides data on retail trade in the central business districts of the important standard metropolitan statistical areas. 

Weekly and monthly estimates of retail sales, monthly estimates of retail far accounts receivable and merchant wholesaler sales and inventories, and yearend inventories held by retailers are parts of the current statistics proatic gram. 

TRANSPORTATION. The first census of transportation is being taken to provide 1963 data on major aspects of transportation including information about out-of-town trips by all modes of travel, manufacturers' shipments by all modes of transportation, truck inventory and use, and financial and operating data on for-hire bus and truck carriers not federally regulated.

FOREIGN TRADE.-Reports on U.S. 

foreign trade include information on imports and exports in commodity and country detail; trade in gold and silver, trade with Puerto Rico and with

U.S. possessions, and trade by custom districts; shipments by vessel and by air; and vessel shipments by port of lading and unlading and flag of vessel. 

GOVERNMENTS.-The census of gov ernments makes available data on numbers and characteristics of governmental units, public employment and payrolls, tax valuations, and governmental finances by type of government. 

The program of current statistics on State and local governments provides annual data on finances and employment and on the financial operations of employee-retirement systems administered by State and local governments, and quarterly data on State-local tax revenue. 

CONSTRUCTION.-Data are compiled monthly on housing starts, value of new construction put in place, new dwelling units authorized by local building permits, national and other aggregates of new residential construction authorized in permit-issuing places, and sales and unsold inventory of new houses.

Statistics are provided yearly on expenditures for residential additions, alterations, and repairs.

GENERAL COMPILATIONS.-With the Social Security Administration's assist ance, the Bureau issues periodically 

County Business Patterns. For addi tional publications, see Appendix B.

INTERNATIONAL STATISTICS.-The 

Bureau provides statistical consultation to foreign governments, arranges orientation programs for foreign visitors, and trains foreign technicians who are studying census and other statistical methods. Special studies are made in the field of foreign population and manpower and international statistical problems and methods. 

FIELD. In addition to collecting data for major censuses and periodic surveys, the field organization conducts special surveys at the request of Federal agencies and State and local governments.

DATA PROCESSING.- -The Bureau has a large data-processing facility for handling statistics from its own censuses and surveys and for assisting other Government agencies with such services at cost. These services include providing computer tapes and punchcards containing machine-readable data, making special tabulations, and assisting in design and alteration of tabulating equipment. Machine-readable data and special tabulations are also made available to the public at cost, under appropriate circumstances.

STATISTICAL STAFF. The Bureau has a staff qualified in the fields of sample survey design and methodology and procedural and program planning. 

This staff performs its functions in Bureau censuses and surveys and acts in an advisory capacity to other Government agencies.

PERSONAL CENSUS RECORDS SERV- 

ICE.-Searches are made of the decennial census records of population and certificates furnished to individuals for use as evidence of age and place of birth. 

Coast and Geodetic Survey  Reg ulations, Title 33, Chapter III]  

Coast and Geodetic Survey was established as the Coast Survey by the act of 

February 10, 1807 (2 Stat. 413), and was redesignated as the Coast and 

Geodetic Survey by the act of June 20, 1878 (20 Stat. 206, 215). The act of 

August 6, 1947 (61 Stat. 788, as amended, 74 Stat. 16; 33 U.S.C. 883a- 

883i), consolidates most of the previous authorizing legislation and sets forth the duties and functions of the 

Coast and Geodetic Survey. 

PURPOSE. The bureau's mission is to provide charts and related information for the safe navigation of marine and air commerce, and to provide basic geodetic, geophysical, and oceanographic data for engineering and scientific purposes and for commercial, industrial, and defense needs.

ORGANIZATION.-The Coast and 

Geodetic Survey headquarters organization consists of the Office of the Director and the following: Office of

Oceanography, consisting of the Op erations Division, Facilities Division, and Marine Data Division; Office of 

Physical Sciences, consisting of the 

Geodesy Division, Photogrammetry Division, Electronic Computing Division, 

Geomagnetism Division, and Seismology Division; Office of Research and Development; Office of Cartog raphy, consisting of the Nautical Chart 

Division, Aeronautical Chart Division, Reproduction Division, and Distribution Division; and Office of Administration, consisting of the Budget and 

Finance Division, Administrative and Technical Services Division, Personnel and Safety Division, Management and Audit Division, and Instrument Divi sion.

FUNCTIONS AND ACTIVITIES.-The 

Coast and Geodetic Survey performs the following activities or functions, including the analysis and processing of the collected data and publication of the results thereof: (1) hydrographic, photogrammetric, and oceanographic surveys, including tide and current observations; (2) geodetic control surveys and the establishment of the basic network of horizontal and vertical control for the United States; (3) other field surveys for nautical and aeronautical charting purposes; (4) geomagnetic, seismological, gravity, and astronomic observations; (5). operation of a seismic sea wave warn ing system serving all Pacific areas; (6) basic research to increase knowledge in the earth sciences and of related space phenomena; and (7) applied research and development in cartography, instrumentation, survey

methods, and processing and analytical techniques, to improve operating efficiency. 

The survey functions enumerated above are accomplished through the operation of survey vessels, mobile field parties, aircraft, observatories and laboratories, and tide gage stations.

In addition, a system of field offices and two ship bases comprise the bureau's field organization. The bureau's = headquarters organization directs and coordinates all field functions and in addition performs the final analysis and processing of the collected data.

The end function performed by the bureau is the reproduction and distribution of the survey results and other collected or discovered knowledge. 

Principal end products include: nautical and aeronautical charts, tide prediction tables, other navigation publications, and geodetic control data in printed form. Besides these, other publications, copies of original records, and special compilations embodying results of regular program work and research in the fields of geodesy, oceanography, cartography, geomagnetism, and seismology are made available. 自然 ​三 ​For

Office of Foreign Commercial Services The Office of Foreign Commercial 

Services was established by the Secretary of Commerce on February 1, 1963, by Department Order 183.

It provides support for all the international programs of the Department of Commerce by carrying out the Department's responsibilities relating to foreign commercial services and commercial officer representation abroad.

Working closely with the State Department to strengthen commercial services within the framework of a unified Foreign Service, the Office implements the provisions of the State- 

Commerce Agreement of November 

1961 on international commercial activities. 

The Office comprises five divisions: 

Overseas Personnel, Foreign Activities Management, Performance Evalua tion, Training Programs, and Foreign Communications. 

As the point of direction or coordination between organization units of the Department of Commerce and the

Department of State and the U.S. 

Foreign Service, the Office performs the following functions: (1) recommends personnel assignments and participates in the selection and control of manpower in the Foreign Service with respect to commercial activities; (2) evaluates the effectiveness of commercial reporting and program operations, and of the performance of personnel assigned to carry out this work abroad; (3) coordinates or initiates improved programs for training commercial officers; (4) coordinates and maintains communications between the Depart ment of Commerce and posts abroad; (5) plans, directs, and coordinates the budgeting, staffing, assignment, recruitment, and related activities of the commercial specialist program as stipulated in the State-Commerce Agreement; and (6) develops guidelines covering the functions and responsibilities of commercial officers abroad, and initiates or coordinates instruc tions to overseas posts.

Bureau of International Commerce  Reg ulations, Title 15, Chapter III]  

Bureau of International Commerce (BIC), center of the Department's international commercial activities, was established by the Secretary on February 1, 1963, by Department Order 

182, under authority provided by Reorganization Plan 5 of 1950. 

BIC promotes the foreign trade of the United States and assists U.S. business in its operations abroad.

PURPOSE. The prime objective of the Bureau is to increase U.S. exports and thus reduce the deficit in the U.S. balance of international payments. It advances this objective by: (1) providing services and information which make it easier for American businessmen to trade abroad; (2) operating trade centers, organizing trade missions, running trade fair exhibits and other marketing devices to promote 

U.S. goods in markets abroad; (3) working with other Government agencies and international organizations to create a climate in which international trade and investment can flourish; (4) presenting the views of traders and investors in governmental councils; and (5) working out policies and procedures which make it simpler and more profitable to do business abroad.

The Bureau also administers the Export Control Act of 1949, as amended (50 U.S.C., App. 2021, 2024) to prevent the export of strategic U.S. materials, equipment, and technical data to Sino-Soviet bloc countries where their use could be detrimental to the 

United States.

The Office of the Director includes the Compliance Commissioner, the Executive Secretariat of the Advisory Committee on Export Policy, the Executive Secretariat of the Foreign- 

Trade Zones Board, and the Interna tional Organizations Staff. There are five other Offices in the Bureau: Commercial and Financial Policy, Interna tional Regional Economics, Interna tional Trade Promotion, International 

Investment, and Export Control.

FUNCTIONS AND ACTIVITIES COMPLIANCE COMMISSIONER.-The 

Compliance Commissioner conducts hearings and performs other duties with respect to administrative compliance proceedings involving export control violation cases.

ADVISORY COMMITTEE ON EXPORT POLICY (ACEP) EXECUTIVE SECRETAR- 

IAT. The Secretariat serves ACEP, the interdepartmental committee established under the Export Control

Act to provide information and advice to the Secretary of Commerce on export licenses, policies, and programs. 

FOREIGN-TRADE ZONES BOARD EXECU- TIVE SECRETARIAT.-This unit conducts regulatory, administrative, and technical affairs of the Foreign-Trade Zones

Board, as required by the Foreign- 

Trade Zones Act (19 U.S.C. 81a-81u) 

which provides for the establishment, operation, and maintenance of foreigntrade zones in or adjacent to ports of entry of the United States.

The zones are sites where foreign and domestic merchandise may be In addition, it administers the China Trade Act of 1922, as amended (15 

U.S.C. 141 et seq.) to promote U.S. 

exports to Hong Kong and Taiwan. 

ORGANIZATION. BIC is headed by a Director who is responsible to the

Assistant Secretary for Domestic and manufacturing, export, re-export, im- 

International Business. brought without being subject to U.S. customs laws governing entry or duties. 

Facilities are available to foreign as well as American business firms. They afford advantages to firms engaged in port, and transshipment.

Six zones and two industrial subzones are operated currently in New 

York, Louisiana, California, Washington, Ohio, and Puerto Rico.

INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS 

STAFF. This is the liaison office for the Department of Commerce with the

Department of State on international organizations. The staff participates in the nomination and selection of U.S. delegates to represent the Department at international conferences, preconference planning and preparation, coordination, and policy review of material for use by U.S. delegations.

OFFICE OF COMMERCIAL AND FINAN- 

CIAL POLICY (OCFP).-This office develops and recommends the Department's international commercial and financial policies and programs. 

It contributes to preparations for and participation in international trade negotiations, advises the President's Special Representative for 

Trade Negotiations on the business interest in reduction in foreign tariff and other trade barriers, and participates in developing the U.S. business interest in the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) and the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD); develops recommendations on foreign tariff concessions, customs valuation procedures, border taxes, and other concessions to be requested of foreign countries; presents the view of the Department and industry in interagency consultations and international negotiating conferences; develops recommendations and participates in international discussions pertaining to international commodity and material policies, marketing arrangements, and commodity study groups; proposes revisions of U.S. Government policies, regulations, and procedures to maintain the competitiveness of U.S. firms in international operations; recommends action to counteract arbitrary and discriminatory treatment of American business; reconciles business needs with U.S. policy aims in the fields of restrictive business practices; presents the American business viewpoint in developing policies for loans and views on specific loans made by the Export-Import 

Bank, Agency for International Development, and international lending organizations; proposes and reviews policies promoting U.S. private investment in less developed countries; insures consideration of export expansion in the development of transportation policy by Government agencies; makes recomendations concerning discriminatory ocean freight rates and other transportation cost factors adversely affecting exports; provides staff sup port to the interagency National Facilitation Committee; and provides advice and assistance to U.S. business in the field of international insurance.

OFFICE OF INTERNATIONAL REGIONAL 

ECONOMICS (OIRE).-This office provides businessmen with information on marketing, investment, and economic conditions in more than a hundred countries and regions; helps established exporters find new business abroad and introduces new or potential exporters to world markets; helps businessmen determine their export potentials by supplying them with data on conditions or policies affecting their ability to compete in particular markets; prepares statistical analyses on trade between the United States and other countries as well as among foreign countries and is the primary source for analyses of trade statistics of foreign countries; and collaborates with the 

Department of State for the removal of foreign government restrictions which make it difficult for U.S. businessmen to compete overseas.

OFFICE OF INTERNATIONAL TRADE PROMOTION (OITP).-This office orga nizes trade centers, trade fair exhibits, and trade missions, and provides other marketing devices and services.

U.S. trade centers located in London, Frankfurt, Bangkok, Tokyo, and

Milan are permanent show-and-sell facilities in overseas marketing areas where interest in buying U.S. made

goods is combined with purchasing power.

U.S. commercial exhibits are staged at international trade fairs abroad to open new markets for U.S. products and to secure overseas agencies for future business.

Interagency exhibitions are organized at international trade fairs in conjunction with the United States Information Agency and other U.S.

Government agencies to demonstrate U.S. social, cultural, and economic accomplishments. 

U.S. trade missions are sent into promising world markets to develop sales and business opportunities for U.S. firms. Official trade missions, each composed of several businessmen and two Commerce Department officers, are organized annually.

Each mission carries hundreds of specific business proposals from American firms directly to businessmen abroad. Trade opportunities developed by the missions are open to all Ū.S. industry.

Mobile trade fair promotion assists U.S. shipping lines in developing mobabile trade fairs.

Cote faire To Business information centers are located at international commercial fairs where it is not feasible to mount a big 

U.S. exhibit. Booths are established through the cooperation of commercial officers in the U.S. Foreign Service. 

Business services provided by OITP include: commercial intelligence to help U.S. firms locate potential customers or representatives overseas; information on foreign distributors, importers, and agents; assistance, with the cooperation of the Foreign Service, in settling trade disputes between U.S. and foreign firms; and the maintenance of an Agency Index to open sales opportunities for overseas representatives of American firms.

OFFICE OF INTERNATIONAL INVEST- MENT (001). This office identifies in vestment opportunities in the developing countries and brings them to the attention of U.S. business; encourages firms abroad to make investments in the United States, especially in areas of heavy unemployment; promotes the licensing of foreign technology to American firms; and publishes for the benefit of American industry opportunities for investment and licensing ventures in the industrialized countries of the free world. 

OFFICE OF EXPORT CONTROL (OEC).— 

This office administers the export control program to keep unfriendly nations from obtaining U.S. commodities or technical data that would contribute significantly to their military or economic potential to the detriment of U.S. security or welfare; uses export controls to protect the domestic economy against excessive drain of scarce materials; conducts educational programs to enlist support of the U.S. business community for effective export control; and investigates suspected violations of export regulations and develops evidence.

Maritime Administration (General Accounting Office Building, 441 G Street NW., Washington, D.C., 20548. 

Phone, STerling 3-5200)  Reg ulations, Title 32A, Chapter XVIII; Title 46, Chapter II; under Office of the Administrator, see Title 32A, Chapter XIX]  

Maritime Administration was established by Reorganization Plan 21 of 

1950, effective May 24, 1950, as one of the successor agencies to the former 

United States Maritime Commission.

PURPOSE.-The Maritime Adminis tration administers programs author-

ized by the Merchant Marine Act, 1936, as amended, and related ship ping statutes to aid in the development, promotion, and operation of an American merchant marine, so that it will be (a) adequate to carry the Nation's domestic waterborne commerce and a substantial portion of its foreign commerce during peacetime; (b) capable of serving as a naval and military auxiliary in time of war or national emergency; (c) owned and operated under U.S. flag by citizens of the United States, so far as may be practicable; and (d) composed of the best equipped, safest, and most suitable types of ships manned by a trained and efficient citizen personnel. 

ORGANIZATION.-The Maritime Ad ministration is headed by a Maritime

Administrator, who is appointed by the President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate. Its headquarters organization in Washington,

D.C., is composed of an Office of Program Planning, Office of Budget and 

Management, Office of Public Information, Office of Statistics, Office of Personnel Management, Office of the General Counsel, Office of the Comptroller, Office of Property and Supply, Office of Ship Construction, Office of Research and Development, Office of 

Ship Operations, and Office of Government Aid. as There is established within the 

Maritime Administration a Maritime 

Subsidy Board, composed of the Maritime Administrator, who serves

Chairman, the Deputy Maritime Ad ministrator, and the General Counsel, each of whom acts pursuant to direct authority from the Secretary of Commerce. The Board makes, amends, and terminates contracts for operating-differential and construction-differential subsidies. It conducts hearings and makes determinations antecedent to these actions; and it investigates and determines the relative costs of constructing ships in the United States and in foreign countries and of operating ships under United States and competitive foreign flags. 

The Maritime Administrator is also vested with the residual powers and authorities of the Director, National 

Shipping Authority, which was estab lished by the Secretary of Commerce on March 13, 1951, for the purpose o organizing and directing emergency merchant ship operations in the national interest. [For regulations codified under National 

Shipping Authority, see Code of Federal Regulations, Title 32A, Chapter XVIII.] 

In the districts, the Offices of the 

Atlantic, Gulf, and Pacific Coast Directors located at New York, N.Y., New Orleans, La., and San Francisco, Calif., are responsible for all field offices and programs of the Maritime Administration within their respective coast areas, except ship construction and maritime training.

FUNCTIONS AND ACTIVITIES GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE TO SHIP- PING.-The Maritime Administration administers the operating-differential and construction-differential subsidy programs and other Government aids to merchant shipping, authorized by law. Under these programs, the Government pays the difference between certain costs of operating ships under 

U.S.-flag and foreign competitive flags, on essential foreign trade routes; and the difference (not to exceed a certain percent of the total cost) between the costs of constructing ships in the 

United States and in foreign shipbuilding centers. The Government also pays the cost of national defense features incorporated in the ships that are certified by the Department of the 

Navy as necessary for national defense.

In addition, the Administration insures mortgages and/or loans made by private lending institutions to finance the construction, reconstruction, and reconditioning of ships; and it acquires old ships in exchange for more mod-

de me al des shind dr eir CON ern and efficient ships or for allowances of credit on the construction of new ships. 

The Administration also investigates and determines ocean services, routes, and lines essential for the development and maintenance of the foreign commerce of the United 

States; and the type, size, speed, and other requirements of ships to provide adequate service on such routes. The operators who are awarded operatingdifferential subsidy contracts are required to maintain regular services on these routes. 

RESEARCH 

AND DEVELOPMENT. 

The Maritime Administration con ducts research and development activities in the maritime field, including cargo handling, development and uti lization of new ship designs, marine transportation systems, advanced propulsion concepts, and ship management techniques. The objectives of this program are to improve the efficiency and economy of operations of the American merchant marine and to promote more rapid technical advancement of it.

SHIPBUILDING AND DESIGN.-The 

Maritime Administration develops plans and specifications for prototype ships. It encourages and participates in the development of plans and designs by subsidized operators under their ship replacement programs, and by applicants for Government aid covering ships proposed to be constructed or converted. It inspects ships during the course of work to assure conformance with approved plans and specifications.

Το carry out the national maritime policy, the Maritime Administration, with the approval of the President, constructs, reconstructs, and reconditions ships for Government account. 

The Administration is authorized to sell these ships, charter them to private operators, or utilize them for Government operation.

SHIP OPERATIONS AND REPAIR. 

The Maritime Administration charters 

Government-owned ships to United States operators when it is determined that such charters will promote the national maritime policy. During national emergencies it requisitions or procures for operation or for charter ships owned by citizens of the United States or under construction, and it determines requirements for and allocates ships to meet the needs of national defense programs. In connection with the foregoing the Maritime Administration prescribes ship operations and ship repair standards and administers such standards under the provisions of charter and general agency agreements and operatingdifferential subsidy contracts.

NATIONAL DEFENSE RESERVE FLEET.-The Maritime Administra tion maintains national defense reserve fleets of Government-owned ships determined by the Maritime Administration and the Department of Defense to be essential for national defense. Ships determined to be nonessential for national defense purposes are sold or otherwise disposed. 

OPERATION OF WAREHOUSES.-The Maritime Administration maintains and operates four warehouses for the storage of marine equipment required for the reactivation, repair, and operation of ships.

RESERVE SHIPYARD.-The Maritime 

Administration maintains a shipyard in an inactive condition to be used for ship construction and repair in national emergencies.

MARITIME TRAINING.-The Maritime Administration operates the U. S. 

Merchant Marine Academy, Kings 

Point, N. Y. Academy graduates are licensed as merchant marine officers and qualified for commissions as en signs in the U. S. Naval Reserve. The 

Administration also administers grant-in-aid program for the five maritime academies operated by five 

States: California, Maine, Massachusetts, New York, and Texas.

CONSTRUCTION RESERVE FUNDS.- 

Under regulations jointly issued by the

778 LIVIVER 

Secretary of Commerce and the Secre tary of the Treasury, American shipowners may deposit proceeds from the sale or loss of ships and earnings from operation of ships in tax-deferred funds, for use in the construction or acquisition of new ships. 

TRANSFER OF SHIPS TO ALIENS.- The Maritime Administration regu lates the sales to aliens, and transfers to foreign registry, of ships owned in whole or in part by citizens of the United States and documented under the laws of the United States, and, in time of war or national emergency, of ships so owned without regard to documentation. 

WAR RISK INSURANCE.-The Mari time Administration is authorized to provide Government war risk insurance of merchant ships when adequate insurance cannot be obtained on reasonable terms and conditions from private insurance companies of the 

United States.

Patent Office was established to administer the patent laws enacted by Congress in accordance with Article. I, section 8, of the Constitution. The first of these laws was enacted April 10, 1790 (1 Stat. 109). General revisions of the patent laws were made on 

July 4, 1836 (5 Stat. 117), and on 

July 8, 1870 (16 Stat. 198). These and other acts of Congress relating to patents were revised and codified, effective January 1, 1953, by the act of 

July 19, 1952 (66 Stat. 792; 35 U.S.C. 

1-293). In addition to the patent laws, the Patent Office administers the Federal trademark laws, the present statute being the act approved July 5, 1946 (60 Stat. 427; 15 U.S.C. 1051, as amended). 

PURPOSE. To administer the patent laws as they relate to the granting of letters patent for inventions, and the trademark laws as they relate to the registration of trademarks. 

ORGANIZATION. The major organi zational units of the Patent Office consist of the Office of the Commissioner of Patents, the Board of Appeals, the Board of Patent Interferences, the Patent Examing Corps, the Office of Administration, the Office of Information Services, the Office of Research and 

Development, the Office of Patent Classification, the Scientific Library; 

with respect to trademarks there is the 

Trademark Trial and Appeal Board, and the Trademark Examining Opera tion. 

FUNCTIONS AND ACTIVITIES.-The 

Patent Office examines applications for patent to ascertain if the applicants are entitled to patents under the law, and grants the patents when they are so en-

Re سلام tock titled; it publishes and disseminates patented matter, records the assignment of patents, maintains a Scientific Library and a search file of U.S. and foreign patents for public use, and supplies copies of patents and official records of the Patent Office. Similar functions are performed in carrying out the statutory provisions for the registration of trademarks.

United States Travel Service 

(1666 Connecticut Avenue NW., Washington, D.C., 20230)

CREATION.-The United States 

Travel Service was established June 

29, 1961, pursuant to the International 

Travel Act of 1961 (75 Stat. 129; 22 

U.S.C. 2121 note) as a primary organization unit in the Department of Commerce.

PURPOSE. The purposes of the 

Travel Service are to develop, plan, and carry out a comprehensive program designed to stimulate and encourage travel to the United States by residents of foreign countries for the purpose of study, culture, recreation, business, and other activities as a means of promoting friendly understanding and good will among peoples of foreign countries and of the United States; encourage the development of tourist facilities, low-cost unit tours, and other arrangements within the United States for meeting the requirements of foreign visitors; foster and encourage the widest possible distribution of the benefits of travel at the cheapest rates between for eign countries and the United States consistent with sound economic principles; encourage the simplification, reduction, or elimination of barriers to travel, and the facilitation of international travel generally; collect, publish, and provide for the exchange statistics and technical information, including schedules of meetings, fairs, and other attractions, relating to international travel and tourism.

ORGANIZATION.-The program of the Travel Service is conducted by the following divisions: Sales Promotion, Media Relations, Facilitation and 

Planning, and Visitor Services. In addition to these divisions, nine overseas offices have been established to stimu late tourist travel. These offices are located in London, England; Paris,

HA LIVIVEN

France; Frankfurt, Germany; Rome,

Italy; Tokyo, Japan; Sydney, Australia; São Paulo, Brazil; Bogotá, Colombia; and Mexico City, Mexico. ap- ACTIVITIES.- -The major share of propriated funds are used to provide tools and materials for distribution by the overseas offices, such as advertisements, pamphlets, brochures, posters, slides, and films, in order to help the prospective traveler study and measure the United States against other competitive destinations. 

In addition, the following activities are being carried out: editorial support of the program through domestic and foreign media endorsing the United States as a tourist destination; encouragement to State and local community groups for the establishment of "host" services throughout the country; development of ways and means of overcoming barriers to travel; and a study of the economic aspects of tourism and patterns of international travel. 

National Bureau of Standards 

(Connecticut Avenue at Van Ness Street NW., Washington, D.C., 20235.

Phone, EMerson 2-4040)  Reg ulations, Title 15, Chapter II] CREATION AND AUTHORITY.—The 

National Bureau of Standards was established by act of Congress of March 3, 1901 (31 Stat. 1449, as amended; 15 

U.S.C. 271-286). The Bureau was initally part of the Treasury Departpment and was transferred to the Department of Commerce and Labor on be its creation in 1903. Unite COLE e en nduce les Pr cilita ervis 

PURPOSE.-The National Bureau of 

Standards is a principal focal point in the Federal Government for assuring maximum application of the physical and engineering sciences to the advancement of technology in industry and commerce. To this end the Bureau conducts research and provides central national services in four broad program areas: (1) basic measurement standards, (2) materials research, (3) engineering standards and applied technology, and (4) radio propagation. 

ORGANIZATION.- -The Bureau is com posed of four major organization units, each of which is concerned with one of the aforementioned program areas. 

These units are: 

(1) The Institute for Basic Stand ards which includes a series of eleven divisions, each serving a classical subject matter area of science and engineering; 

(2) The Institute for Materials Re search which consists of six divisions organized primarily by technical field; 

(3) The Institute for Applied Tech nology which includes a technology center, six technical divisions, and a clearinghouse for scientific and technical information; and 

(4) The Central Radio Propaga tion Laboratory which comprises a series of four divisions located at Boulder, Colo. 

FUNCTIONS AND ACTIVITIES INSTITUTE FOR BASIC STANDARDS.- 

This institute provides the central basis within the United States of a complete and consistent system of physical measurement, coordinates that system with the measurement systems of other nations, and furnishes essential services leading to accurate and uniform physical measurements throughout the Nation's scientific community, industry, and commerce. 

Its principal activities include the development and maintenance of the national standards for physical measurement; determination of fundamental

physical constants; research on fundamental physical phenomena; research and development on measurement techniques and instrumentation; and the calibration of instruments in terms of the national standards. 

INSTITUTE FOR MATERIALS RE- 

SEARCH.-This institute assists and stimulates industry in the development of new and improved products by supplying increased understanding of the basic properties and behavior of materials and making available reliable quantitative information on the performance of materials. These functions are accomplished through research on the properties of matter and materials; the development of techniques for the preparation of experimental materials and for the measurement of their properties; the development of criteria to evaluate the performance characteristics of materials, and the development, production, and distribution of standard reference materials. 

INSTITUTE FOR APPLIED TECHNOL- 

OGY.-This institute provides special industry oriented technical services to facilitate and encourage the use by industry of available technology and to stimulate technological innovation. 

The main functions of the Institute are to identify and evaluate obstacles to technical innovation in industry; develop a technical basis for the evalu ation of technological products and services; maintain continuous cooperation with public and private organizations leading to the development of technological standards such as codes, methods of test, and engineering standards; and to provide a central clearinghouse for the collection and dissemination of scientific and technical information from domestic and foreign sources.

CENTRAL RADIO PROPAGATION LABO- RATORY.-The Laboratory is the cen tral agency of the Federal Government for the collection, analysis, and dissemination of information on the propagation of radio waves along the surface of the earth, in the atmosphere, and in phere, and in space, and performs studies looking toward new techniques for the efficient use and conservation of the radio spectrum. The Laboratory conducts basic research on the nature of radio waves and the media through which they are transmitted; studies radio propagation mechanisms; provides advisory services on radio frequency utilization and radio systems; and issues predictions of radio propagation conditions. 

Weather Bureau (M Street bet. Twenty-fourth and Twenty-fifth Streets NW., Washington D.C., 20235.

Phone, 965-2400)  

Regulations, Title 15, Chapter V] CREATION AND AUTHORITY.-An act of October 1, 1890 (26 Stat. 653; 15 

U.S.C. 311), established the United

States Weather Bureau in the Depart ment of Agriculture. The President's Reorganization Plan IV of 1940 trans ferred the Bureau and its functions to the Department of Commerce. Additional legislation and executive decisions have broadened the Bureau's activities, emphasized its responsibility for providing basic weather services to support all Federal agencies and user interests (particularly civil aviation), and authorized the use of space satellites for meteorological purposes.

PURPOSE. The Weather Bureau is responsible for the national meteorological service. This service includes reporting the weather and climate of the United States and its possessions, and issuing forecasts and warnings of

62 weather and flood conditions that affect the Nation's safety, welfare, and economy. 

ORGANIZATION.—Approximately 325 

field offices are operated by the 

Weather Bureau at cities and airports throughout the United States, in Puerto Rico, and on some of the islands of the Pacific Ocean. In addition, more than 12,000 substations, most of them staffed by volunteers observers, provide less complex reports and observations to supplement those taken by the principal Weather Bureau offices. 

Ocean weather stations are maintained by the Bureau in both the Atlantic Grand Pacific Oceans and in the Gulf of Mexico. tion Lew ted Supervision of field stations in the United States is exercised through Regional Administrative Offices located dat New York, N.Y.; Fort Worth, Tex.;

FUNCTIONS AND ACTIVITIES.-To carry out its statutory responsibilities, the Weather Bureau:

Maintains basic networks of weather-measuring stations, makes weather analyses and forecasts, and conducts climatic studies and archiving work. 

Provides public warnings, forecasts, and related information concerning the weather of the United States and adjacent waters. In the interest of safety and economy, the Weather Bureau also provides forecasts and warnings for aviation, agricultural, and forest-protection interests.

Issues flood warnings, river stage forecasts, and water supply forecasts covering most of the principal rivers and tributaries of the United States. 

Collects, analyzes, and publishes information concerning the climate of the United States, the oceans, and certain foreign areas. 

Conducts basic and applied meteorological research to improve weather warnings and forecasts. This includes studies of worldwide wind circulation, cloud physics, atmospheric processes, and other meteorological phenomena, as well as research aimed at improving meteorological instruments and weather communications systems. 

Has the responsibility of establishing and operating a satellite system for the continuous observation of worldwide weather systems. Information received from weather satellites is processed and disseminated to users in the United States and the international community. Approved.

Department of Labor, ninth executive department, was created by act approved March 4, 1913 (37 Stat. 

736; 5 U.S.C. 611). A Bureau of

Labor was first created by Congress in 1884 under the Interior Department. The Bureau of Labor later became independent as a Department of Labor without executive rank. It again returned to bureau status in the Department of Commerce and Labor which was created by act of February 

14, 1903 (32 Stat. 827; 5 U.S. C. 591).

Additional duties related to the statutory functions of the Department of Labor subsequently have been assigned to the Department by new legislation and by Executive order.

PURPOSE.-The Department of La bor is charged, among other things, with administering and enforcing statutes designed to advance the public interest by promoting the welfare of the wage earners of the United States, improving their working conditions, and advancing their opportunities for profitable employment. 

ORGANIZATION.-All functions of the 

Department are vested in the Secretary of Labor. The structure of the 

Department is shown in the organization chart which appears on page 587.

for Legislative Affairs coordinates, supervises, and directs all legislative activities of the Department including contracts with the Congress and presentation of legislative programs and views to the Congress.

WAGE APPEALS BOARD.-The Wage Appeals Board acts on behalf of the 

Secretary of Labor in deciding appeals on questions of law and fact, taken in the discretion of the Board (1) from wage determinations issued by the Solicitor under the Davis-Bacon Act and its related prevailing wage statutes; (2) debarments under the Department's regulations Part 5 (29 CFR Part 5), which implement Reorganization Plan 14 of 1950; (3) under the

Department's regulations, Part 5, disputes concerning the payment of prevailing wage rates or proper classifications which involve significant sums of money, large groups of employees, or novel or unusual situations; and (4) recommendations by Federal agencies for appropriate adjustments of liqui dated damages which are assessed under the Contract Work Hours Standards Act. 

Under Secretary of Labor The Under Secretary of Labor is the alternate of the Secretary in the discharge of all the Secretary's responsibilities. He serves as Acting Secretary in the Secretary's absence.

The Office appraises the manpower requirements and resources of the and Nation and develops policies, objectives, and standards to deal with the problems of persistent and other types of unemployment and underemploypment, while considering such factors ple as current and prospective manpower shortages, dislocations in the economy arising from automation or other technological developments, foreign competition, relocation of industry, shifts in market demands, and other changes in the structure of the economy. 

The Office is responsible for plan ning and coordinating an overall pro- 715-681-64—21 gram of manpower research and statistics, for conducting research, and arranging for other bureaus of the Department, other Government agencies, and private agencies to conduct research and related statistics programs.

The objective is to identify the many ramifications and the dimensions of the manpower problems of the Nation and to seek through research, adequate solutions to these problems. It plans and directs developmental and experimental studies in all areas of manpower and automation to find solutions to problems which significantly affect the Nation's ability to eliminate persistent and other types of unemployment and underemployment and to evaluate the impact of and benefits and problems created by automation and other forms of technological progress. It plans and develops a program to increase and expand knowledge of how occupational competence that will aid in eliminating unemployment and underemployment is achieved.

The Office prepares materials for the President's and the Secretary of

Labor's Annual Manpower Reports together with recommendations for action. It prepares the Secretary of 

Labor's annual report to the Congress

on training and research activities conducted pursuant to the Manpower Development and Training Act of 1962, as amended, including an evaluation of the effectiveness of such activities. It provides technical manpower information to the public, professional groups, unions, employers, and Government agencies on the nature of manpower problems and programs. It maintains a clearinghouse of technical and research information on manpower, automation, and training. 

The Office coordinates the program planning and development activities of the Department of Labor bureaus providing manpower programs for the aging, minority groups, the handicapped and youth, and insures that the bureaus and offices providing manpower programs take into account the occupational interests, circumstances, and operations of women in the labor force. 

The Office is responsible for evaluating plans, programs, progress, and results of the elements of the comprehensive manpower program; examining and reporting on special difficulties which interfere with achievement of general objectives; and providing appraisals of the adequacy of programs to meet foreseeable manpower needs. 

Bureau of Apprenticeship and

Training 

The National Apprenticeship Act was passed in 1937 to bring together employers and labor for the formulation of programs of apprenticeship. 

The Bureau of Apprenticeship and Training carries out the objectives of the act in conformance with policies determined by the Federal Committee on Apprenticeship, an 11-member committee appointed by the Secretary of Labor and composed of 5 represent atives each from management and labor and 1 from the U.S. Office of Education. 

The Bureau promotes the establishment and improvement of apprenticeship and other on-the-job training programs and provides technical as sistance and training aids where necessary. Its functions are to aid management and labor in recognizing the need for apprenticeship. Through field representatives in each State the Bureau works closely with employers, labor, vocational schools, and others concerned with apprenticeship programs throughout industry. Bureau of Employment Security 

[For regulations codified under this head ing, see Code of Federal Regulations, Title 20, Chapter V] 

The Bureau's responsibilities are related to the administration of a nationwide system of public employment services, State unemployment insurance programs, Federal unemployment compensation programs, and special manpower programs designed to relieve the effects of unemployment and to promote maximum utilization of the Nation's manpower. The legislative bases for the Bureau's operations include the Wagner-Peyser Act, the 

Federal Unemployment Tax Act, titles III, IX, XII, and XV of the Social Security Act, title V of the Agricultural 

Act of 1949, and various provisions in the Immigration and Nationality Act, the Area Redevelopment Act, the 

Manpower Development and Training Act, and the Trade Expansion Act. 

Because the Bureau is responsible for the Government's interest in carrying out the mission of the employment security system, its operations cover a wide range of activities, both as a Federal entity and in providing leadership to the State employment security agencies. It coordinates employment security action with other Govern ment agencies and the public, and advises the legislative and executive branches on employment security matters. It plans programs on a nationwide basis. To enable sound program planning, it collects and analyzes operational and economic data, which in published form provide Government, labor, management, and the public with information of value in assessing economic trends and developments.

The Bureau conducts evaluations of the administration and operation of 

State employment security agencies. 

This involves the measurement of achievements, the making of recommendations for improving State administrative operations and management, and the provision of assistance in the establishment of improved methods of administration and operation. 

Fiscal responsibilities involve justification of appropriation requests before Congress, allocation of funds among States, establishment of standards for expenditures, auditing of State fiscal accounts and records, filing of exceptions on funds improperly expended, review of applicable State laws and their execution, and certification of such laws to enable the allocation of Federal funds for administrative costs.

The Bureau provides leadership to the State employment security agencies, involving responsibility to: (1) develop and interpret national policies and goals; (2) study program needs and administrative problems; (3) develop techniques, tools, and measures for improvement in administration and program content; (4) promote adoption of improvements in State legislation and administration;

and (5) provide continuing technical assistance and interchange of experience and information.

The Bureau works closely with State agencies in the development and maintenance of a well-selected and trained personnel staff. It develops methods for the selection, training, and management of employment security staff.

This coordination enables widespread research, testing, and validation of techniques. From such coordinated effort have come such products as the Dictionary of Occupational Titles, occupational tests, and occupational job descriptions. 

The Bureau also actively participates in mobilization planning and in the preparation being made by the Federal Government for national emergencies which might arise. In addition, the Bureau coordinates civil defense and mobilization activities in 

State employment security agencies.

The eight regional administrators of the Bureau whose offices are nearest to those of the Office of Emergency Plan ning have been given responsibility for carrying out the Department's manpower mobilization activities in the field.

These overall responsibilities are in addition to specific responsibilities for the two basic programs, as described below. 

The Bureau's employment service program responsibilities, as assigned to its United States Employment Service under the provisions of the Wagner- Peyser Act, include assistance in estab lishing and maintaining systems of public employment offices in the States and territories; assistance in coordinating such systems throughout the coun try and increasing their usefulness by developing and prescribing minimum standards of efficiency; collecting and furnishing information as to opportu nities for employment and other infor mation of value in operating the systems, including information about labor market developments by area (and classification of areas according to relative labor supply), by industry, by occupation, and for agriculture; maintaining a public employment service for the District of Columbia, a veterans' service devoted to securing employment for veterans, and a farm placement service; and maintaining a system for clearing labor among the 

States. The United States Employ ment Service guides and assists the States in placement functions, occupational analysis, counseling, and testing functions; in maximizing employment opportunities for veterans, older workers, youth, handicapped workers, members of minority groups, and workers affected by the impact of automa

174 tion and changing technology in promoting community efforts toward the greatest possible use of the labor force; in promoting use by employers of the public employment service; and in providing materials and techniques to employers for effective use of manpower.

The United States Employment 

Service has cooperative arrangements with Selective Service in counseling, testing, job development, and training of educationally deficient rejectees. It also has arrangements with the Department of Defense to assist in the reorientation of military retirees before and after retirement. A new youth program gives greater job development and employment assistance to youth, including the disadvantaged and school dropouts. 

Because of the demand for professionally trained and highly skilled workers the Employment Service, under the direction of the President and in the Congress, has strengthened its placement service for job seekers in professional and technical occupations, utilizing its nationwide system of interarea recruitment.

Since 1961 the United States Emdeployment Service has been given additional responsibilities in carrying out operational aspects of various Federal acts designed to develop and utilize the Nation's manpower resources. Under the Area Redevelopment Act it obtains facts needed for determining eligibility of areas, reviews manpower aspects of oevrall economic plans for these areas, determines occupations for which training programs may be required, and selects and refers individuals for training. Under the Manpower Devel opment and Training Act the Employ ment Service determines training needs, selects and refers trainees, develops job opportunities, refers trainees to jobs, and follows up placements of trainees. Under the Trade Expan sion Act it assists eligible persons in finding suitable employment and in obtaining appropriate training. Its role in the Public Works Acceleration Act is to obtain facts needed to determine the areas which are eligible for assistance, and to select and refer workers to contractors and agencies on projects. 

The United States Employment 

Service has an active part in the Vocational Education Act of 1963. In order to qualify for Federal funds, each

State must submit through its State board to the Commissioner of Education a plan which provides for entering into cooperative arrangements with the public employment offices in the State, relating to occupational information, guidance, training, and placement.

Under the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952, the United States Employment Service, with the assistance of the State employment security offices, reviews and makes determinations on requests for the importation and employment of alien workers to assure that in cases approved, the alien workers will not displace, nor adversely affect the wages and working conditions of, workers in the United States similarly employed.

The Office of Farm Labor Service develops policies and procedures for and directs and coordinates a service for agricultural workers and employers which will provide adequate placement facilities for meeting year-round and seasonal labor requirements of agriculture and to place individual workers seeking employment in agriculture and to provide for the orderly and expeditious seasonal movement of migrant workers to successive jobs by providing placement service and current and reliable information regarding crop conditions and employment opportunities. The Office also is responsible for insuring that in the interstate recruitment of farm workers applicable standards are met relating to housing, transportation, and wages. 

The Office also administers responsibilities under the act of July 12, 1951

The Bureau's unemployment insurance program responsibilities include review and analysis of State laws and constructions thereof to determine if they are in conformity with the Social 

Security Act and the Federal Unem ployment Tax Act; review of State administration of unemployment insurance to determine whether the program is in compliance with the provisions of State law necessary to meet the 

Federal requirements, and whether individuals are denied benefits to which they are entitled under the State law and under the various agreements with the Secretary of Labor to carry out the 

Federal Unemployment Compensation

programs;

establishment of feasible criteria for measuring administrative costs for use in determining the in determining the amounts of money necessary for proper adapting improved administrative procedures developed by the Bureau and efficient administration of the 

State unemployment compensation laws; and furnishing assistance to the States on administrative and operating problems, in applying or adapting improved administrative pro- 1cedures developed by the Bureau or by individual States, and in developing legislative recommendations designed to improve the program under the economy of each State. The 

Bureau also analyzes past trends and forecasts future trends in coverage, contributions, benefit rights, and benefit payments State by State and in the 

Nation as a whole; studies and recommends methods of improving the unemployment insurance program; disseminates information on the operation of the unemployment insurance program; assists the States in conducting studies of the effect of proposed program changes as well as their current programs, and in preparing evaluations of the solvency of the 

States' unemployment insurance benefit funds, as well as of the continued adequacy of the States' reserves and tax structures in light of actual or proposed amendments to the laws and the expected future incidence of unemployment; studies and develops policy recommendations concerning other governmental or private incomemaintenance programs which may affect the unemployment insurance system; directs the administration of a 

Federal program to pay allowances to workers who are undergoing approved training; and develops plans for the emergency payment of unemployment allowances in situations of enemy attack or national disaster. 

The Federal Advisory Council on 

Employment Security, composed of representatives of employers, employees, and the public, was established by the Wagner-Peyser Act "to discuss problems and develop policy recommendations relating to employment and unemployment, and to insure impartiality, neutrality, and freedom from political influence in the solution of such problems." The Council advises the Secretary of Labor and the Administrator of the Bureau with respect to the administration and coordination of the functions of the Bureau.

Both acts authorize the conduct of the Labor-Management Reporting investigations and the initiation of civil and Disclosure Act of 1959 (73 Stat.

The Welfare and Pension Plans Dis closure Act provides for the reporting and disclosure of information concerning the operation of welfare and pension plans and the bonding of persons handling such plans, provides specific power to investigate complaints and to secure compliance and restrain violations of the law through civil judicial proceedings, and to issue binding and authoritative opinions and interpretations.

The Labor-Management Reporting and Disclosure Act provides for the reporting and disclosure of certain financial transactions and administrative practices of labor organizations and employers; the prevention of abuses in these areas and in the administration of trusteeships by labor organizations; and the enforcement of standards and procedures with respect to the election and removal of officers of labor organizations. and criminal legal actions.

The Office is under the direction and supervision of a Director, appointed by the Secretary of Labor, who receives, analyzes, and makes available submitted for public disclosure reports by those covered by the acts, including labor organizations, their officers and employees, employers, welfare and pension plan administrators, etc.; provides technical assistance and advice to persons or groups concerned with reporting under the acts; recommends rules and regulations and communicates interpretations necessary to carry out the acts; and directs investigations and promotes compliance with the acts. 

These functions are carried out by a national office in Washington, D.C., and by a nationwide network of regional and area offices. [For regulations codified under Office of 

Labor-Management and Welfare-Pension

Policy planning and development responsibilities of this office include: review of the performance of collective bargaining and its contribution toward meeting current economic and social needs; development of objectives for

Wage and Hour and Public Contracts Divisions 

[For regulations codified under this head ing, see Code of Federal Regulations, Title 29, Chapter V; Title 41, Chapter 50] The Wage and Hour Division was established pursuant to the provisions of the Fair Labor Standards Act of 

June 25, 1938 (52 Stat. 1060; 29

Administrator, appointed by the President with the consent of the Senate. 

The Fair Labor Standards Act of 

1938, as amended, establishes, subject to specified exemptions, minimum wage, overtime compensation, and child labor standards for employees

L who, on an individual basis, are engaged in interstate or foreign commerce, including any closely related process or occupation directly essential thereto. The act also applies to any employee in an enterprise engaged in commerce or the production of goods for commerce, as defined in the law, including employees handling, selling, or otherwise working on goods that have been moved in or produced for commerce.

CO d P 

The Equal Pay Act of 1963 requires employers on and after June 11, 1964, to pay equal wages within an establishment to men and women doing equal work on jobs requiring equal skill, effort, and responsibility which are performed under similar working conditions. The effective date of the equal pay standard is deferred for employees covered by collective bargaining agreements until the termination date of the agreement, but in any case not later than June 11, 1965.

The Walsh-Healey Public Contracts 

Act requires Federal Government supply contracts in amounts exceeding $10,000 to contain stipulations with respect to payment of minimum wages and overtime, nonemployment of child and convict labor, and observance of certain safety and health standards.

Bureau of International Labor Affairs 

The Bureau was established on December 31, 1959, replacing the Office of International Labor Affairs origi nally established in 1947. Under the policy direction of the Assistant Secretary of Labor for International Affairs, the Bureau is headed by an Administrator who is responsible for discharg ing Department of Labor functions in the international labor field. Under the policy direction of the Assistant Secretary, the Administrator is also charged with mobilizing, directing, and coordinating all other international activities of the Department's various specialized offices and bureaus. 

These functions and responsibilities of the Bureau include advising on the implications of international labor developments in developments in relation to U.S. foreign and domestic policy, analyz ing the impact of domestic policy and developments on labor aspects of foreign affairs, recommending 1121*111* 1 WEL

operations designed to promote the United States national interest in the foreign labor field generally and with respect to specific areas of the world, and, with the assistance of other offices and bureaus, operating programs affecting labor which are designed to implement foreign policy. 

The Bureau's staff of geographic area specialists develops detailed action programs in the field of labor for the various foreign countries. Through these country programs, the Government's efforts are coordinated to achieve U.S. foreign policy objectives as they relate to labor abroad. 

The Department of Labor has primary responsibility, under the overall foreign policy guidance of the Department of State, for United States participation in the International Labor

Organization. 

The Bureau also carries out the Department's responsibilities for assisting the Department of State in the management of the Foreign Service, including the labor attaché and Foreign

Service labor-reporting programs (the 

Department has statutory membership on the Board of the Foreign Service); for representation on delegations and formulation of labor policy in connection with United States participation in the United Nations Economic and

Social Council and its various commissions; for participation in the 

Trade Staff Committee and other interagency trade expansion activities and for staff support for the Department's representatives on the Trade

Expansion Act Advisory Committee and the Trade Executive Committee; and for participation of labor missions in the Government's international trade fair program. In these activities the Bureau relies upon technical assistance from other bureaus of the Department.

The Bureau coordinates and directs programs, both its own and those of other bureaus, which are carried on by the Department under various acts of 

Congress and under administrative agreements with other agencies for development of a fund of labor and manpower knowledge for use both in domestic and overseas programs; for development of a reservoir of labor and manpower experts; and for programs of technical cooperation and exchange of persons. As requested, consultants are supplied for foreign assignments, technical materials are furnished for use abroad, and training programs are conducted in the United States for foreign nationals. These programs are implemented in cooperation with the Department's bureaus and regional offices, State departments of labor, American trade unions, management, and other private organizations. 

The Bureau's responsibility for advice on the implications of international labor developments in relation to 

United States foreign and domestic policy calls for a continuing program of analysis of such labor developments and their economic and social implications in foreign countries. This program, as well as the other international programs of the Department, call for active and current research on foreign labor developments. In this connection, great reliance is placed upon the 

Division of Foreign Labor Conditions of the Bureau of Labor Statistics, which is responsible for research on labor around the world.
