Public Health Service 

Regulations, Title 42, Chapter I]  Public Health Service has its origin in an act of July 16, 1798 (ch. 77, 1 Stat. 

605), authorizing marine hospitals for the care of American merchant seamen. Subsequent legislation has vastly broadened the scope of its activities. 

The Public Health Service Act of 

July 1, 1944 (58 Stat. 682; 42 U. S. C. 

201), consolidated and revised substantially all existing legislation relating to the Public Health Service, including title VI of the Social Secu rity Act, and provided for greater assistance to States, for coordinated el research, for establishment of a national tuberculosis control program, and for expansion of the commissioned the corps. The basic Public Health Serv- 

Dice legal responsibilities have been broadened and expanded many times since 1944. nofth o pot WEL ddres Among the more important functions added have been those for the da control and prevention of water pollution and air pollution; expanded fellowship and training programs; loans to students in the health professions; grants to States for planning comprehensive mental retardation programs; and the administration of construction grants for hospitals and medical facilities, waste treatment works, health research facilities, teaching facilities for health personnel, research centers and other facilities for the mentally retarded, and mental health centers.

PURPOSE. The Public Health Serv ice, under the direction of the Surgeon 

General, is the Federal agency specifically charged with responsibilities for protecting and improving the health of the people of the Nation. It is also responsible for collaborating with governments of other countries and with international organizations in world health activities. The major functions of the Service are: (1) to conduct and support research and training in the medical and related sciences, and in public health methods and administration; (2) to provide medical and hospital services to persons authorized to receive care from the Service, to aid in the development of the Nation's hospital and related facilities, and to prevent the introduction of communicable diseases into the United States and its possessions; and (3) to assist the

States and other governments in the application of new knowledge for the prevention and control of disease, the maintenance of a healthful environment, and the development of community health services.

ORGANIZATION.-The activities of the Service are organized into four bureaus: Office of the Surgeon Gen eral, Bureau of Medical Services,

Bureau of State Services, and National 

Institutes of Health; and the National

Library of Medicine. 

The National Advisory Health 

Council and the advisory councils established for each major program area provide overall advice and policy guidance to the Surgeon General and review all research grant applications in their area of competence. Advice and consultation is also secured from other advisory groups, from the Board of Regents of the National Library of 

Medicine, and from the Conference of

State and Territorial Health Officers. 

In order to maintain direct contact with State and local authorities, with field offices of other Federal agencies, and with other official and nonofficial

BASES $1 

organizations concerned with its activities, the Service maintains a staff in the regional offices of the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare. 

These staffs are headed by regional health directors who represent the Surgeon General in interpreting and carrying out the broad policies of the 

Service. The regional health director is assisted by two associate regional health directors, one representing the programs of community health and the other, the programs of environmental health. The regional staffs work with 

State authorities in developing and maintaining plans, programs, and budgets for Federal-State cooperative health programs. 

Office of the Surgeon General The Office of the Surgeon General is a bureau composed mainly of staff services for the three operating bureaus and for the Surgeon General in his overall management of the organization. Its various divisions and offices assist in (1) studying the health needs of the Nation; (2) coordinating grant policies of the Service; (3) promoting the communication of scientific information; (4) providing overall program and policy direction to Service activities in the international health field and in the planning, negotiation, and administration of Service responsibilities for international health services with Federal agencies and international organizations; (5) directing and coordinating the Service's information, publications, and public inquiries programs; (6) developing general plans and programs under which personnel administration will be carried on within the Service; (7) managing budget and fiscal activities; (8) carrying out a comprehensive internal audit program; (9) providing for the management of all areas of general services; (10) facilitating organizational and procedural improvements and the general management of the Service; (11) supervising

Public Health Service regional organizations and coordinating Public Health 

Service Federal-State activities; and (12) preparing the Nation to meet the health and water needs of the civilian population in the event of a national disaster. 

THE NATIONAL CENTER FOR HEALTH STATISTICS.-The Center serves as the principal statistical arm of the Public Health Service and one of the major general purpose statistical organizations of the Government. This organization conducts continuing surveys and special studies of the Nation's population to determine the extent of illness and disability and to gather information related to these conditions.

Areas of interest include the amounts and type of medical services received, the economic and social impact of illness and disability and methods of financing family health care. Such information establishes a current picture of the Nation's health and serves as a basis for predicting health trends.

The Center is also the principal instrument of Federal Government cooperation with the States in the collection of vital statstics (births, deaths, marriages, and divorces) and is the only source of national tabulation and analysis of such data. The Center also sponsors cooperative studies in foreign countries which provide useful comparative statistical data. 

Bureau of Medical Services

The Bureau of Medical Services is the medical arm of the Public Health

Service primarily concerned with developing and directing certain medical care and health services programs, and preventing the introduction of disease and the entry of mentally and physi cally defective aliens into the United States. 

Medical care is provided eligible beneficiaries through a system of Public Health Service hospitals, outpatient clinics, and offices located throughout the United States where seamen employed on vessels of U.S. Registry,

Sen al& Pub med Coast Guard and other uniformed services personnel, and other legal beneficiaries receive hospitalization, medical and dental care, and preventive health services. In addition, dependents of uniformed services personnel are entitled to medical care and emergency dental care at such hospitals and outpatient clinics. A program of therapeutic and preventive health services is provided for Indians and Alaska natives of the United States through area and field offices operating PHS Indian and Alaska native hospitals, health centers, school health centers, practical nurse training schools, and health stations; and through contracts with local governmental and nongovernmental resources. By direction of the Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare, administrative supervision is provided Freedmen's Hospital in the District of Columbia. This is a general hospital for the treatment of acute medical and surgical conditions, with an extensive system of specialized clinics for outpatients. The hospital provides internship and clinical experience for medical students and graduates of Howard University. [For regulations codified under Freedmen's Hospital, see Code of Federal Regula tions, Title 42, Chapter IV] 

Public laws and regulations to prevent the introduction of quarantinable and other dangerous communicable diseases into the United States are implemented through a system of worldwide epidemiological vigilance and inspection of arriving persons, animals, and things at ports and airports involved in international traffic. The medical provisions of the Immigration and Nationality Act to exclude persons who present a danger to public health or a probability of an economic burden to public funds are implemented by medical examinations of aliens performed abroad, and by medical inspections at ports of arrival. 

Technical advice and personnel are furnished to assist other Federal agen- 715-681-64- -23 cies in health care programs for their employees and beneficiaries. Professional supervision and consultation are provided Service personnel directing medical care programs and/or performing medical services for certain other Federal agencies. Presently, personnel of the Public Health Service, assigned to this Bureau, administer medical care programs for other Fed eral agencies as follows: by law-Bureau of Prisons and the U.S. Coast 

Guard;

by interagency agreement— 

Bureau of Employees' Compensation in the Department of Labor.

Bureau of State Services 

The Bureau of State Services is the principal operating bureau of the Service for Federal-State and interstate health programs. It gives general direction to activities in the two broad areas of Community Health and Environ mental Health designed to aid the States and communities in developing, establishing, and maintaining effective programs for the prevention, treatment, and control of diseases and for the prevention or control of environmental health hazards.

Within these areas, the Bureau conducts research; provides training; furnishes consultation and technical assistance to States and localities; conducts field surveys, investigations, and demonstrations; provides emergency disaster and epidemic aid to States; enforces corrective measures under certain statutes; conducts public information and education programs; and administers various grant and student loan programs. 

COMMUNITY HEALTH.-Bureau pro grams in this area are concerned with: (1) the development of techniques for the application of scientific observations in the fields of biology and medicine; (2) the social and behavioral aspects of major health problems; (3) the organization and delivery of comprehensive community health services, including the health services for domes-

tic agricultural workers and their families; (4) the development and effective utilization of professional, technical, and supplementary manpower; and (5) the planning and construction of hospitals and related medical facilities appropriate to the needs of communities. These programs include the control of chronic diseases such as heart disease, cancer, diabetes, and arthritis; the control of communicable diseases (including tuberculosis and veneral diseases) and the eradication of certain disease vectors; the conservation of sight, hearing, and speech and the control of mental retardation and other neurological disorders; the development and coordination of community health programs to remedy and alleviate problems of the aged; the provision of consultation on nursing home and noninstitutional care services; the administration of health programs in the fields of nursing services and resources; dental services and resources; and accident prevention; the support and conduct of research, experiments, and demonstrations relating to the development, utilization, and coordination of services, facilities, and resources of hospitals and other medical facilities including a construction program for such facilities (Hill-Burton Act). 

ENVIRONMENTAL HEALTH.-Bureau programs in this area are concerned with: (1) the conduct and support of research to determine the nature, methods for effective measurement, and the health effects of environmental contaminants, including the total or cumulative effect as well as the individual effects on man; (2) the development of techniques and methods for practical control programs and for the maintenance of a healthful environment; (3) the study of political, social, and economic factors related to urbanization and metropolitan complexes as they affect environmental health, in order to develop effective methods of organization and administration in this field; (4) the development and effective utilization of professional and technical manpower and other resources for the broad field of environmental health; and (5) the administration of interstate quarantine regulations, and air and water pollution control enforcement measures. 

These programs include air pollution control; water supply and water pollution control; milk, food, shellfish, interstate and community sanitation; occupational health; radiological health; and arctic health; with research centers at Cincinnati, Ohio, and Anchorage, Alaska, as well as specialized operational activities at numerous field stations located throughout the country. 

National Institutes of Health 

The National Institutes of Health, the principal research arm of the Public Health Service, is primarily concerned with the extension of basic knowledge regarding the health problems of man and how to cope with them.

Fundamental laboratory and clini cal research in causes, prevention, and methods of diagnosis and treatment of cancer, cardiovascular and geriatric diseases, allergy and infectious dis eases, arthritis and metabolic diseases, dental diseases and conditions, mental illnesses, and neurological and sensory diseases, is conducted by the National 

Cancer Institute, National Heart In stitute, National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, National In stitute of Arthritis and Metabolic Dis eases, National Institute of Dental Re search, National Institute of Mental

Health, and National Institute of Neu rological Diseases and Blindness, respectively. Patient facilities which service the clinical investigations programs of the Institutes are provided by the Clinical Center.

Grants-in-aid to public and nonprofit institutions and to individuals including research, training, and field investigations grants-in the general

Leve be of medical and health related sciences, and in maternal and child health and the basic sciences relating to the process of human growth are provided by the National Institute of General 

Medical Sciences and the National 

Institute of Child Health and Human 

Development, respectively, and by the other Institutes in the categorical areas of their interest. Fellowships are provided to individuals by the same organizational units. 

The Division of Research Grants is responsible for the overall review and coordination of the grants programs for all the institutes and divisions of the National Institutes of Health. 

The Division of Research Facilities and Resources makes grants-in-aid for health research facilities construction, and other across-the-board institutional grant programs for primate centers, general clinical research centers, special resource centers, and general research support. 

The Division of Biologics Standards administers the provisions of the Public Health Service Act that require the licensing of establishments and and specified biological products when they are intended for sale, barter, or exchange in interstate commerce, or for export from or import into the 

United States. alert the nal B ute d Ni of De 

The Division of Research Services provides facilities, equipment, and a wide variety of scientific, technical, and supportive services essential to the needs of the medical investigator and research administrator at the National 

Institutes of Health. 

The Office of International Re search carries out the Service's increasing responsibilities in international medical research. 

National Library of Medicine The National Library of Medicine comprises the greatest collection of medical literature in the world, exceeding a million pieces. The Library was established to assist the advancement of medical and related sciences, and to aid the dissemination and exchange of scientific and other information important to the progress of medicine and to the public health. The Library acquires and pre serves books, periodicals, and other library materials; organizes these materials by appropriate cataloging and indexing; publishes bibliographical guides to medical literature; encourages the publication of biomedical scientific materials for better access to medical information and to improve international communications; and provides reference and research assistance. 

Office of Education 

Regulations, Title 45, Chapter I]  

Office of Education was created by act of March 2, 1867 (14 Stat. 434; 20

U.S.C. 1). In 1869 the Office of Edu cation became a part of the Department of the Interior; it was transferred to the Federal Security Agency upon that Agency's creation in 1939; and it became a constituent agency of the Department of Health, Education, and

Welfare upon the establishment of that 

Department in 1953.

PURPOSE.--The statutory functions of the Office of Education are to collect such statistics and facts as shall show the condition and progress of education, to diffuse such information as shall aid the people of the United States in the establishment and maintenance of efficient school systems, and otherwise to promote the cause of edu cation. Subsequent acts and Executive orders have added related functions, including responsibilities for Federal

financial assistance to education and for special studies and programs. 

ORGANIZATION.-The Office of Edu cation includes the Office of the Commissioner and three operating bureaus: 

Bureau of Educational Research and 

Development, Bureau of International

Education, and Bureau of Educational Assistance Programs. A fourth operat ing bureau, the Bureau of Higher Education Facilities, has been approved for establishment.

Office of the Commissioner The Office of the Commissioner is composed of the immediate Office of the Commissioner and four staff of fices: Office of Program and Legisla tive Planning, Office of Administration, Office of Information, and Office of Field Services. These staff offices provide staff services for the Commissioner and for the three operating bureaus.

Bureau of Educational Research and Development 

The Bureau of Educational Re search and Development, which includes the Office of the Associate Commissioner and six divisions, is responsible for programs dealing with the identification of major problems in education, the collection and dissemination of information about education, the support of research conducted by public and private institutions, and assistance to the profession and the public in solving educational problems. 

The Division of Educational Statis tics collects, analyzes, and publishes statistics on education at all levels; and administers a program of grants to States to improve and strengthen statistical services of State educational agencies. 

The Division of Educational Re search administers contracts with universities, colleges, and State educational agencies for research and demonstrations in education; administers contracts and grants for research and dissemination in the use of modern communications media for educational purposes; and provides captioned films for the deaf.

The Division of Higher Education conducts studies and provides consultative services in the field of higher education; makes an annual inspection of Howard University; cooperates with the Veterans Administration in certain relations with State approv ing agencies and prepares a list of nationally recognized accrediting agencies and associations; approves educational institutions for attendance by aliens under student visas; authenticates certificates validating the American academic credentials of foreign students; and provides advisory serv ices to the Housing and Home Finance 

Agency on college housing loans.

The Division of Elementary and Secondary Education conducts studies and provides consultative services in educational administration and in curriculum and instruction for elementary and secondary schools; assists in the establishment of science clubs for boys and girls; and assist in the administra tion of the Juvenile Delinquency and

Youth Offenses Control Act of 1961. 

The Division of Continuing Educa tion and Cultural Affairs adminsters the program for the extension of library services under the Library Services and supplementary acts; and conducts studies and provides consultative services in the fields of adult education and cultural facilities and programs.

The Division of Handicapped Chil dren and Youth conducts studies and provides consultative services in areas related to the education of handicapped children; administers grant programs for training professional personnel in the education of children who are mentally retarded, hard of hearing, deaf, speech impaired, visually handi-

Home! fort cluts! he linge Acto capped, seriously emotionally disturbed, crippled, or otherwise health impaired; and administers grants for research and demonstration projects in these areas. 

Bureau of International Education The Bureau of International Edu ication, which includes the Office of the Associate Commissioner and two divisions, provides leadership in the field of international education.

The Division of International 

Studies and Services makes studies of education in foreign countries; provides advisory interpretations of foreign academic credentials to educational institutions, State educational agencies, licensing boards, and civil service commissions; prepares teaching aids about other countries for use in 

United States schools; and provides technical services for international organizations and conferences.

The Division of Technical Assist ance and Exchange Programs recruits 

American educators for service abroad under the United States technical as sistance (AID and UNESCO) pro grams; recruits teachers for duty overseas under the Fulbright-Hays Act and participation in summer seminars abroad; arranges programs of study and observation for foreign teachers and school administrators and other leaders under the international educational exchange program and the technical assistance program; maintains a clearinghouse of information on exchange and performs related research; and promotes modern foreign language training and area studies.

Bureau of Educational Assistance 

Programs 

The Bureau of Educational Assist ance Programs, which includes the 

Office of the Associate Commissioner and four divisions, administers many of the financial assistance programs of the Office. 

The Office of the Associate Com missioner, besides providing general administrative services for the bureau, administers a grant program for the construction of television broadcasting facilities to be used for educational purposes. 

The Division of Vocational and Technical Education administers the Vocational Education Act of 1963, and the Smith-Hughes, George-Barden, and supplementary acts, which provide grants to the States for encouragement and financial support of State operated vocational and technical training programs; administers a program of grants to States for development of area vocational education programs in scientific or technical fields; provides financial assistance for occupational training in redevelopment and other areas; and provides consultative and leadership services in all relevant areas of vocational and technical education. 

The Division of School Assistance in Federally Affected Areas administers a program of financial assistance in the construction of school facilities and in the maintenance and operation of schools in areas affected by Federal activities; and provides financial assistance to the Dade County, Fla., public schools for the education of Cuban refugees. 

The Division of State Grants ad ministers a program of grants to States and loans to nonprofit private schools for the purchase of equipment for and the improvement of State supervision to strengthen elementary and secondary school instruction in science, mathematics, and modern foreign languages; and provides grants to States to strengthen guidance, counseling, and testing for students not below grade 7 in elementary or secondary schools. 

The Division of College and University Assistance administers Federal grants for land-grant colleges under the Morrill and supplementary acts; administers a program of Federal par-

ticipation in college and university student loan funds; provides fellowships for graduate study; administers a program of contractual arrangements with institutions of higher education to establish institutes to improve the qualifications of secondary school guidance and counseling personnel; contracts for the operation of modern foreign language institutes and centers and for the conduct of research in foreign language teaching and learning; and administers programs of loans and grants to institutions of higher education for the education of Cuban refugees. 

Bureau of Higher Education

Facilities 

The Higher Education Facilities Act of 1963 authorizes a program of financial assistance to institutions of higher education to construct classrooms, laboratories, and libraries in order to accommodate mounting student enrollments and to meet demands for skilled technicians and for advanced graduate education. Current planning envisions the administration of this program by a Bureau of Higher Education Facilities, which has been approved for establishment.

Social Security Administration 

 Reg ulations, Title 20, Chapter III]  Social Security Administration, under a Commissioner for Social Security, was established by the Federal Security Administrator pursuant to Reorgani zation Plan II, effective July 16, 1946, which abolished the Social Security Board (see appendix A) and transferred its functions, along with functions of the Children's Bureau, to the 

Federal Security Administrator. Dele gated to the Commissioner for Social Security were functions in connection with old-age and survivors insurance, unemployment insurance, and public assistance, and most maternal and child welfare programs. Other duties have subsequently been delegated to or transferred from the Administration by law or Presidential order.

The position of Commissioner for Social Security was reestablished as 

Commissioner of Social Security in the 

Department of Health, Education, and

Welfare by Reorganization Plan 1, effective April 11, 1953. The Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare on

January 28, 1963, reorganized the 

Social Security Administration, estab lishing the old-age, survivors and disability insurance (OASDI) and Federal credit union programs as the primary missions of the Administration.

The Bureau of Old-Age and Survivors 

Insurance was abolished as a bureau and the Bureau of Family Services and the Children's Bureau were transferred to a new Welfare Administration.

PURPOSE.-The Social Security Ad ministration administers the Federal old-age, survivors and disability insur ance programs (title II of the Social 

Security Act, as amended, and title VII and XI of that act as they pertain to the Social Security Administration), and the Federal credit union program 

(Federal Credit Union Act). It is responsible for studying problems of poverty and insecurity and the contributions that can be made to their solution by social insurance and related programs and for making recommendations for the most effective methods of improving social and economic security through social insurance. 

The purpose of old-age, survivors and disability insurance (OASDI) is to provide continuing income for individuals and their families as partial replacement of earnings lost through old-age or disability retirement or death. The OASDI program provides

for the coverage of almost all persons engaged in gainful employment, including the military, the major exceptions being Federal civilian employees under a retirement system; selfemployed doctors of medicine; and domestics, agricultural workers, and self-employed persons having very low earnings. Entitlement to benefits is determined from the insured status of the a individual; the age and relationship of the individual and his dependents; the application for such benefits; and en in the case of disability benefits, the extent and expected duration of disability. Benefits are payable monthly in amounts related to the average monthly earnings of the insured person. A lump sum death benefit is payable under certain conditions.

RE The Federal credit union program promotes thrift by encouraging cooperative, systematic saving and by making credit available in the short-term, small loan field at reasonable rates of interest, for credit union members. To accomplish these purposes, Federal credit unions provide convenient facilities for encouraging the development of habits of consistent regular saving out of current earnings.

CENTRAL ORGANIZATION.-The So cial Security Administration is composed of the Office of the Commissioner and 11 components. Ten of these provide administration of the 

OASDI program of the Social Secu rity Act, while the eleventh, the Bureau of Federal Credit Unions, administers the Federal credit union program. The ten OASDI organizations are: the Divisions of Management, the Actuary, Claims Policy, Program Evaluation and Planning, Research and Statistics,

Accounting Operations, Claims Con trol, Disability Operations, Field Operations, and the Bureau of Hearings and Appeals.

REGIONAL AND FIELD ORGANIZA- 

TION.-To the greatest extent consistent with effective and uniform administration, operations of the Social 

Security Administration are decentral ized to provide services at the local level to persons covered by the OASDI program, to its beneficiaries and claimants for benefits, and to persons who appeal OASDI decisions. Eleven social security regional representatives supervise the activities of 613 district offices concerned with operations of the 

OASDI program. Seven regional hear ings representatives of the Bureau of 

Hearings and Appeals provide admin istrative direction to hearings examiners located in cities throughout the country, who hold hearings and render decisions (under the provisions of the 

Administrative Procedures Act) in connection with appeals of OASDI de terminations. Likewise, localized service in connection with chartering, supervising, and examining Federal credit unions is provided by the 10 regional representatives of the Bureau of Federal Credit Unions and their staffs.

Office of the Commissioner The Office of the Commissioner in cludes the immediate Office of the 

Commissioner, the Central Planning

Staff, and the Office of Information. 

The Commissioner of Social Secu rity, except for certain functions which remain with the Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare, is responsible for administering the old-age, survivors and disability insurance program. 

This includes policy determination, administration of research programs in social insurance, program interpretation, and providing recommendations on methods of advancing economic security through social insurance. The Commissioner is also responsible for the administration of the 

Federal Credit Union Act. 

The Executive Director assists and acts for the Commissioner in giving overall executive leadership to the activities of the Social Security Ad ministration and acts for the Commis-

sioner during the absence or disability pares a variety of reports for adminof the Commissioner. 

The Executive Assistant assists the

Commissioner and Executive Director in the formulation of major policy and in the provision of executive leadership to assure effective implementation of policy. He acts for the Commissioner and Executive Director in implementing the policies and values of the Commissioner in wide areas of organization leadership and direction. In the absence of both the Commissioner and the Executive Director he carries out the functions of the Office of the Commissioner to assure continuity of all 

SSA operations and activities.

The Central Planning Staff is responsible for leading and coordinating

SSA efforts to achieve improved systems, procedures, and organization of work effort.

The Office of Information plans and directs a nationwide program of public information to provide public understanding of rights and responsibilities under Social Security programs. It develops guidelines and techniques applicable to all informational media, and produces a wide range of materials to serve these media; conducts surveys and studies to identify problems and to determine the effectiveness of informational activities; and provides staff direction to SSA's public correspondence activities. 

OASDI Organizations The Division of Management pro vides the full range of management staff services to the Commissioner in the management and supervision of the component organizations of SSA. 

The Division of the Actuary pre pares long- and short-range cost estimates involving such factors as population structure and mortality, morbidity, wage, employment, and retirement trends in connection with present and proposed social security programs; conducts actuarial studies; and preistrative use and for publication. 

The Division of Claims Policy develops and recommends retirement and survivor insurance program policies; evaluates existing policy and develops recommended changes; and issues substantive instructions and interpretive materials to provide basic broad program direction for the claims and benefit processes. With the Division of

Disability Operations it develops coordinated policies and procedures of mutual concern and application to the retirement, survivors, and disability insurance processes. It plans and coordinates the issuance of Social Security 

Regulations, the Social Security Handbook, Social Security Rulings, Compi lation of Social Security Laws and re lated issuances for internal and public use; participates in legislative planning; and represents SSA in negotiation and coordination activities in assigned fields.

The Division of Program Evaluation and Planning evaluates the effectiveness of the present OASDI program provision; clarifies and interprets the objectives of the program; evaluates and develops legislative recommenda tions; and provides technical and advisory services to congressional committees and individual Congressmen.

The Division of Research and Sta tistics plans and conducts long-range research in the general area of human resources and the economic security of the American family; develops extramural cooperative research in social security under a cooperative research and demonstration grants program; carries out continuing research in such areas of study as family economics, medical economics, international social security, and statistics oriented both to meeting OASDI program and administration needs and to providing bases for meeting the needs of a wide range other governmental agencies, research organizations, universities, and scholars. The Division plans, develops, and of

directs the conduct of large data collection operations related to basic studies of economic and social conditions of the total population. 

The Division of Accounting Opera tions establishes and maintains records of the identity of all holders of Social Security account number cards. It receives and records earnings reports data, investigates erroneous reports and earnings discrepancies, and makes necessary adjustments. It also maintains employer identification number records. The Division furnishes duplicate account number cards and OASDI earnings and status information, upon request, for title II purposes; certifies earnings record data for claims purposes; and provides statistical data for program and administrative analyses. 

The Division of Accounting Operations operates a large data processing and a data transmission facility and provides computer service for other parts of SSA as well as for its own operations. 

The Division of Claims Control su pervises the operations of seven payment centers which are responsible for: the certification of all benefit payments under title II of the Social Security 

Act, as amended; the authorization and reconsideration of OASI claims; the adjustment and discontinuance of benefit payments; the recovery or waiver of overpaid amounts; the investigation of continuing eligibility of beneficiaries and the assessment of penalties for violations of the reporting provisions of the act; and the identification of cases involving possible fraud.

The Division also develops, adjudicates, and authorizes OASDI benefit claims filed by persons residing in foreign countries, and determines the continuing eligibility of such persons. 

The Division of Disability Opera tions develops and recommends policies relating to the determination of disability under the Social Security 

Act; evaluates existing policy and develops recommended changes; and issues substantive instructions and interpretive materials to provide basic broad program direction to the disability determination processes and for relating those processes to rehabilitation services. It coordinates with the 

Division of Claims Policy on policies and procedures of mutual concern and application to the retirement, survivors, and disability insurance processes. It formulates management standards and policies for State agencies operating under contractual agreements, and administers, with the assistance of the social security regional representatives, a management program to guide, control, and evaluate State agency operations, including the determination of fiscal requirements and allocation of operating funds for each State agency. The Division reviews State agency disability determinations, authorizes payment or disallowance of benefits in disability cases, and makes disability determinations in cases not covered by State agreements. 

It represents SSA in disability program coordination and negotiation with other Federal, State, and private organizations, and with the medical profession. It participates in legislative planning, and acts as SSA consultant on disability policy matters. 

The Division of Field Operations supervises the operations of the social security regional and district offices which are responsible for: developing public understanding of the purposes and provisions of the OASDI program and of the public's rights and responsibilities thereunder; assisting the public in filing claims for OASDI benefits; developing and adjudicating claims; conducting investigations relating to earnings records, coverage, and fraud in order to insure accuracy of benefit payments; informing beneficiaries of events which may affect benefit payments, and providing necessary assistance in making appropriate reports; providing effective referral services to other agencies within the community (e.g., rehabilitation, public welfare, legal aid); issuing social security account numbers; and coordinating areas

of mutual program or operating interests with Federal, State, and local governmental and private organizations. 

The function of the Bureau of Hearings and Appeals is to provide impartial and independent hearings and reviews to persons who wish to contest determinations as to their OASDI rights made in the usual course of the 

Administration's operations. A total of 175 hearings examiners are located in cities throughout the country. The examiners are independent of and not responsible to any regional or headquarters official of any component or ganization of the Social Security Ad ministration other than those of the 

Bureau of Hearings and Appeals. They are located in space separate from SSA district offices. Administrative direction and substantive assistance is provided them by regional hearings representatives who are responsible to the central office of the Bureau. That office consists of the Director, the Deputy 

Director, six members of the Appeals

Council, and an administrative and program staff. The Appeals Council, on which the Director sits as chairman and the Deputy Director as deputy chairman, provides a level of review above that of the hearing examiners. 

On its own motion or on request of appellants, it may review-with authority to revise, reverse, or remandthe decisions of hearing examiners. 

Bureau of Federal Credit Unions 

[For regulations codified under this head ing, see Code of Federal Regulations, Title 45, Chapter III] The Bureau of Federal Credit Un ions was established within the Federal 

CREATION AND Security Agency by act of July 29, 1948 

(62 Stat. 1091; 14 U.S.C. 751a) to assume functions of the Federal Credit

Union System (see appendix A). The 

Bureau, by Department order, functions as a program bureau of the Social 

Security Administration subject to the direction of the Commissioner of Social

The Bureau, through its Federal credit unions, provides a further market for securities of the United States and makes more available to people of small means credit for provident purposes through a national system of cooperative credit, thereby helping to stabilize the credit structure of the 

United States.

A Federal credit union is a cooperative association organized for the purpose of promoting thrift among its members and creating a source of credit for provident or productive purposes. 

To accomplish these purposes Federal credit unions provide convenient facilities for encouraging the development of habits of consistent regular saving out of current earnings. From the fund of members' savings, installment loans of limited size are made to members at rates of interest which must not exceed 

1 percent a month on the unpaid balance. The responsibility for operation and management of each Federal credit union rests with officials who are elected by its members.

The Bureau's field program of chartering, examining, and supervising credit unions is conducted by a staff of trained examiners who are supervised, respectively, by 10 regional representatives, who in turn report to the 

Director of the Bureau of Federal

Credit Unions. 

Welfare Administration AUTHORITY.-The 

Secretary's reorganization of January 28, 1963, created the Welfare Administration and assigned to it the following components and their pro grams: the Bureau of Family Services, the Children's Bureau, and the Cuban

Refugee Program Staff from the Social Security Administration; and the Of fice of Aging and the Office of Juvenile mik i

Delinquency and Youth Development from the Office of the Secretary; together with administration of titles VII 

and XI of the Social Security Act as they apply to the Welfare Administration.

PURPOSE.-The Welfare Adminis tration is responsible for administering the programs of the Federal Government pertaining to assistance to individuals and families in need, the provision of welfare assistance and services for children, the aging, and other groups, and maternal and child health services. It is responsible for studying the causes, prevention, and reduction of dependency, matters pertaining to child life, the welfare needs of children, the aging and other groups, and for making studies and recommendations as to the most effective method of providing social and economic security through social welfare programs. The programs are primarily Federal State in nature, with the States receiving Federal grants-in-aid in return for operating in accordance with Federal standards. In the welfare areas of research, demonstration projects, consultation, stimulation, and coordination the relationships of the Welfare Administration extend to State, local, and voluntary agencies, community groups, and universities.

CENTRAL ORGANIZATION.-The Welfare Administration includes the Office of the Commissioner, the Cuban Refugee Program Staff, the Office of Aging, the Office of Juvenile Delinquency and Youth Development, the Bureau of 

Family Services, and the Children's Bureau.

REGIONAL AND FIELD ORGANIZA- 

TION.-A regional representative and appropriate supporting staff is assigned to each of the Department's nine regional offices for each of the following program areas: family services, child welfare, maternal and child health, and aging. These regional staffs are established to provide consultation and services to State and local agencies and organizations in their program areas, and, to the maximum extent consistent with effective management, to provide decentralized program administration. 

Office of the Commissioner

The Office of the Commissioner directs and coordinates the Welfare Administration program and performs basic research covering the broader phase of social welfare. This includes the formulation of policy, coordination of interprogram activities, review and coordination of administrative management activities, and certification of compliance with State laws, plans, and operations with Federal requirements, and approval of grants to States. 

The Office of the Commissioner provides training services for fellows and scholars from other countries, cooperates in overseas projects through recruitment of experts and continuing technical supervision, participates in research and other technical exchange with international organizations and with other countries, and assists in the preparation for international meetings on subject matter of concern to the 

Welfare Administration. 

The Office of the Commissioner also formulates broad research and statistical goals and policies, conducts the basic studies necessary to analyze aspects of social welfare that are beyond the immediate scope of the bureaus, and reviews and integrates the statistical and analytic work of program bureaus. Its activities are concentrated on overall social, financial, and economic aspects, the relation of the programs to other social welfare and related measures, and the development of findings and recommendations on the most effective methods of providing social and economic security through social welfare programs. The 

Office of the Commissioner also provides a secretariat for making contracts with or grants to States and public and

other nonprofit organizations and agencies for paying part of the cost of research or demonstration projects in the field of social welfare and related programs. 

Cuban Refugee Program Staff The Cuban Refugee Program was established in accordance with the 

President's letter to the Secretary dated

January 27, 1961, and continues under the Migration and Refugee Assistance Act of 1962 (76 Stat. 121; 22 U.S.C. 

2601 note) and Executive Order 11077 

of January 22, 1963. The Staff admin isters an emergency program which includes: (1) financial assistance to supply basic essentials (food, clothing, and shelter) to needy refugees; (2) financial assistance in relocating refugees from Miami, Fla., to homes and jobs elsewhere in the country and overseas; (3) emergency health services; (4) assistance to the public schools of 

Dade County (Miami, Fla.) in providing instruction to the refugee children as well as English instruction and vocational training to adults; (5) loans to refugee students in college and funds for English and refresher courses for doctors and other professional persons; and (6) care of minors unaccompanied by relatives. These programs are carried out through a Federal Cuban 

Refugee Emergency Center in Miami, four voluntary relocation agencies, and a variety of Federal, State, and local agencies and organizations. 

Office of Aging 

This office conducts a continuing review and analysis of program needs, activities, and accomplishments in the field of aging. It acts as a focal point for the coordination of all aging activities of the Department. It provides stimulation, guidance, and counseling to the States and to local agencies and organizations in this field, and serves as principal DHEW liaison with other Federal departments and agencies on aging matters. 

Office of Juvenile Delinquency and Youth Development 

This office was established to carry out the demonstration project and training grant program provided in the 

Juvenile Delinquency and Youth Offenses Control Act of 1961 (75 Stat. 

572; 42 U.S.C. 2541 note). It operates a grant and contract program for the partial support of demonstration proj ects aimed at the prevention and control of juvenile delinquency and a program to train personnel who work in the field of juvenile delinquency. Proposed studies and projects are reviewed and selected for support in terms of their promise in helping to overcome the present fragmented approaches to dealing with the problem. This review is continued during the period of the selected studies and projects to assure that continued support is appropriate. 

Bureau of Family Services 

[For regulations codified under this head ing, see Code of Federal Regulations, Title 45, Chapter II] The Bureau of Family Services, which until January 1, 1962, was known as the Bureau of Public Assistance, administers grants to help States provide public assistance under the 

Social Security Act for old-age assist ance and medical assistance for the aged (title I), aid to the blind (title 

X), aid to families with dependent children (title IV), and aid to the permanently and totally disabled (title 

XIV), and aid to the aged, blind, or disabled, or for such aid and medical assistance for the aged (title XVI).

The Bureau reviews and approves 

State plans for public assistance; reviews State estimates, and certifies to the United States Treasury Federal grants to the States; reviews the oper ation of State plans for continuing conformity with the Social Security 

Act; collects, analyzes, and publishes data on the operation of public as sistance in the States, including general assistance, and provides technical help to States to improve their programs.

Public assistance includes financial aid, medical care, and other social services to help recipients achieve their potentialities for self-care, self-support, and strong family life. The extent of financial aid and the provision of services vary between States, reflecting the

State's traditions, legislative and administrative structures, community concern, and assistance appropriations.

The State plan must provide for the program to be in effect in all parts of the State, and for State financial participation. A single State agency must administer the program or supervise its administration. The plan must provide for such methods of administration, including a merit system covering personnel, and for submitting such reports as the Department finds necessary for and efficient proper operation.

The plan must provide for keeping personal information confidential (except as modified by section 618 of the 

Revenue Act of 1951, 65 Stat. 569). 

It cannot set residence and citizenship requirements beyond those named in the Federal law. It must provide for a hearing before the State agency for those who are not satisfied with the ac- -tion on their cases. In determining need and the amount of the payment, the State must take into account any other income or resources of the person claiming aid. In aid to the blind, some of the blind person's earned income is disregarded, and in medical assistance for the aged, a reasonable amount of income and resources is permitted as determined by each State. 

The Social Security Act defines the scope of Federal participation, but does not limit the breadth of State operations. The State may claim Federal money to help needy people living in their own homes, in private insitutions, and in public medical institutions (except patients in institutions beyond 42 days after a diagnosis of tuberculosis or psychosis). The State's payments to assistance recipients for maintenance must be in the form of money. Some medical costs are included in the money payment but most are paid by the agency directly to the medicalcare suppliers. 

Under assignment, the Bureau is responsible for assisting the States in developing and maintaining plans for a state of readiness for welfare services in a civil defense emergency, and for continuity and restoration of peacetime welfare programs; performs welfare planning activities in regard to refugees and immigrants, and the repatriation of American nationals from abroad. 

Children's Bureau [For regulations codified under this head ing, see Code of Federal Regulations, Title 42, Chapter II] 

The Children's Bureau was created by the act approved April 9, 1912 (37 

Stat. 79, as amended; 42 U. S. C. 191 et seq.) (see also appendix A). 

On January 28, 1963, the Bureau was transferred from the Social Security Administration to the new Welfare

The purpose of the Bureau is to investigate and report on all matters related to child life and to increase opportunity for the full development of all children by promoting their health and social welfare. It administers title 

V of the Social Security Act. 

The Bureau cooperates with national, State, and local organizations and agencies, both public and voluntary, in planning for the development and extension of services for children and youth.

In carrying out the responsibilities assigned by its organic act, the Bureau makes studies of conditions that are a hazard to the well-being of children, and of the effectiveness of measures aimed at preventing and alleviating such conditions. On request, it gives advisory service to State and local

agencies regarding research and methods of conducting programs aimed at promoting the health and welfare of children. The Bureau provides a clearinghouse of research in child life by collecting and distributing information regarding research studies under way in universities, schools, hospitals, child research centers, and other public and private agencies throughout the country. In addition, it provides child welfare research and demonstration grants for projects which are of regional or national significance and for demonstration of new methods or facilities which show prom- ise of substantial contribution to the advancement of child welfare.

The Bureau issues both technical and popular publications. Most widely known of its publications for parents is Infant Care. Its Statistical Series presents data on operations of child health and welfare programs and statistics on the conditions of child life. 

For a representative list of publications, see appendix B.

The Bureau administers, through its 

Division of Health Services, grants to 

State health agencies for extending and improving health services for mothers and children, authorized by title V, part 1, of the Social Security Act. 

These agencies use the funds to provide health promotion services such as maternity clinics for prenatal and postnatal care of mothers; pediatric clinics; well-child clinics for supervision of the health of children under school age by physicians, assisted by public health nurses and other professional and technical workers in the health field; health services for school children, including health supervision by physicians, dentists, public health nurses, and nutritionists; dental care for children and pregnant women; and programs for mentally retarded children. The Bureau provides medical, dental, nursing, nutrition, physical-therapy, and medical-social consultation services to State health agencies administering such services. 

Through its Division of Health Serv ices, the Bureau administers, a 5-year program of grants to provide maternity and infant care, authorized by title V, part 4, of the Social Security Act. State health agencies or, with the consent of such agencies, the health agencies of any political subdivisions of the States use these grants to provide medical care to women who during the maternity period are unlikely to receive necessary health care because they are from families with low incomes or for other reasons. In addition to medical care for the mother, health care for mothers and infants following childbirth is included. The health care is available particularly to prospective mothers who have or are likely to have conditions associated with childbearing which increase the hazards to the health of mothers or their infants, including those which may cause physical or mental defects in the infants.

The Bureau also administers, through its Division of Health Services, grants to State crippled children's agencies for extending and improving services for crippled children, authorized by title V, part 2, of the Social 

Security Act. These agencies, usually in State health or welfare departments, use the funds to provide medical, surgical, corrective, and other services and care for children who are crippled or suffering from conditions that may lead to crippling and to provide facilities for diagnosis, medical care, hospitalization, and after-care for these children. 

The Bureau provides consultation service to the State agencies on methods and procedures for the early casefinding, the diagnosis, and medical treatment of crippled children and on the development of programs for the care of children with special types of crippling conditions such as epilepsy, poliomyelitis, rheumatic fever, congenital heart disease, and cerebral palsy.

to The Bureau administers, through its Division of Social Services, grants to State public welfare agencies, authorized by title V, part 3, of the Social Security Act, to establish, extend, and strengthen child welfare services. In each State public welfare agency, the division responsible for services to children plans and directs the program for child welfare services. Federal funds are used mainly for State staff members to assist in the development of community child welfare programs, for child welfare workers in local communities to provide social services to children, for training of child welfare staffs, and for foster care for certain children who are the responsibility of public welfare agencies. In the administration of these grants the regional staff of the 

Division of Social Services participates in the development of State plans and gives advisory and consultant service to State public welfare agencies. 

Specialists develop guide materials and provide consultation to national, State, and local public and voluntary agencies in developing services to children in their own homes, foster family care, group care, and institutional care; adoption services; homemaker services; day care services; services to unmarried mothers; and services to mentally retarded children as well. 

Specialists also advise on training of staff in child welfare programs and on State legislation relating to children. 

Child welfare training grants may be used by accredited institutions of higher learning to expand and strengthen their resources for classroom and field teaching to prepare students to work in the field of child welfare; for traineeships for students interested in the field of child welfare; and for support of short-term training courses. 

The Bureau offers technical assistance in the field of juvenile delinquency to States and communities planning the extension, improvement, and more effective coordination of the various State and local services and facilities required for the location, treatment, and rehabilitation of delinquent youth. Consultants are available to advise on the training of personnel for these services; on the content, legislative bases, and administration of juvenile delinquency programs; and on such special types of services as police, juvenile courts, detention, diagnostic and reception centers, training schools, and group work. The Division of Juvenile De linquency Service develops standards and guides; makes surveys of services and facilities; cooperates with States and localities; and collaborates with voluntary organizations on the development of programs and the training of personnel for services for juvenile delinquents.

The Children's Bureau is the technical agency in the U.S. Government which acts as consultant and adviser to the International Children's Fund.

The Bureau also has working relationships with the UN and its related agencies such as the World Health 

Organization, as well as with voluntary international organizations working in the field of child life.

The Bureau provides information on services for children in the United

States in response to requests from international bodies and from other countries. The Bureau carries responsibility for recruiting and for providing technical help to specialists in maternal and child health and child welfare who are sent to other countries under the United States Government technical-assistance program. It also carries responsibility for developing programs of study and observation for specialists from other countries desiring to study maternal and child health and child welfare services for children in the United States.

The Children's Bureau is advised in its work by committees and conference groups called to consider special problems.

Vocational Rehabilitation Administration 

Regulations, Title 45, Chapter IV]  Office of Vocational Rehabilitation, redesignated Vocational Rehabilita tion Administration on January 28, 1963, was created to administer the expanded program of State-Federal vocational rehabilitation provided by the Barden-LaFollette Act of July 6, 

1943 (57 Stat. 374; 29 U.S.C. 31 note), which amended the Vocational

Rehabilitation Act of June 2, 1920 (41 

Stat. 735; 29 U.S.C. 31 note). Other duties have been delegated to the Administration pursuant to the Voca tional Rehabilitation Amendments of 1954 (68 Stat. 652; 29 U.S.C. ch. IV) 

and subsequent legislation or Presidential order.

PURPOSE.- -The services of vocational rehabilitation are provided for the purpose of developing, preserving or restoring the ability of disabled men and women to perform useful work. The Vocational Rehabilitation 

Administration cooperates with the

States in providing these services. The mentally as well as the physically handicapped may receive rehabilitation services. 

ACTIVITIES.-The States have broad authority and responsibility in carrying out their programs of vocational rehabilitation. The States may now, at their option, either continue their rehabilitation programs under their boards of vocational education or place them under separate agencies concerned primarily with rehabilitation.

In each State which has a separate agency to serve the blind, this agency may function as the sole State agency responsible for administering that part of the State plan relating to rehabilitation of the blind. 

Strong cooperative relationships are encouraged between State agencies for vocational rehabilitation and all other agencies such as public employment services which provide services needed in the vocational rehabilitation and job placement processes. 

Within the Federal Government, coordinated planning by the Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare and the Secretary of Labor is required to develop and recommend to appropri ate State agencies policies and proce dures which will promote the employment of disabled men and women who have received services under the rehabilitation program. In addition, the 

Secretaries of these two Departments are directed to work with the Chairman of the President's Committee on

Employment of the Handicapped in developing methods to secure the maximum use of services of the Committee and its cooperating State and local organizations in promoting employment opportunities for the disabled. 

The Vocational Rehabilitation Ad ministration is responsible for the establishment of standards in the various areas of service; for the approval of 

State plans and amendments; for technical and professional assistance to the 

States; for certification of Federal grants-in-aid to the States and public or other nonprofit organizations and agencies; for making studies, demonstrations, and reports, disseminating information, and providing short-term training and instruction on matters relating to vocational rehabilitation; and for designating the State commis sion or other agency serving the blind to license blind persons to operate vending stands on Federal or other property. Consultation assistance is given the States on a continuing basis by regional representatives of the 

Vocational Rehabilitation Administra tion. Rehabilitation services include thorough medical diagnosis to determine the extent of disability and possibilities

of improvement to discover possible hidden disabilities, and to determine work capacity; necessary medical, surgical, psychiatric, and hospital treatment; necessary prosthetic devices such as artificial limbs, hearing aids, and braces; individual counseling and guidance; training for jobs; maintenance, training materials, and transportation during rehabilitation, if necessary; occupational tools, equipment, and licenses; placement in the right job; and adjustment services until the mutual satisfaction of worker and employer are assured. The States and Territories purchase rehabilitation services, as required, from existing public or private facilities. Medical and other examinations, counseling, training (in most States), and placement services are provided without cost to the individual. All other services are provided without cost to the extent that clients cannot pay for them.

All men and women with substantial job handicaps in the form of physical or mental impairments are eligible for services. Three conditions generally must exist before a State rehabilitation agency provides services: (1) a disability which substantially interferes with employment, (2) a reasonable chance of becoming suitably employed, and (3) an employable age (or near it).

Federal grants authorized and appropriated are matched by State and local funds. 

The disability insurance provisions of the Social Security Act provide for disability insurance payments to qualified disabled workers and their dependents and for disabled children of a retired or deceased worker. They also provide that applicants for such benefits must be referred to the State vocational rehabilitation agencies for vocational rehabilitation services to the end that as many of them as possible may be returned to gainful employment. The act further provides that disability payments may be reduced or 715-681-64-24 suspended for beneficiaries who, without good cause, refuse rehabilitation services. The State vocational rehabilitation agencies in all but five States are making disability determinations in the cases of applicants for benefits under Federal law and regulations pursuant to agreements with the Social 

Security Administration. 

The vocational rehabilitation program is in effect in the 50 States, the 

District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, the 

Virgin Islands, and Guam. There are now 90 State agencies in all, 48 under

State boards of vocational education, 6 independent agencies, and 36 agencies serving only the blind.

The Vocational Rehabilitation Ad ministration is responsible for (1) a program of training for professional personnel and (2) research to advance knowledge of ways of overcoming handicapping conditions. For the training of professional personnel the Administration conducts a program of training grants to public and voluntary educational institutions and agencies and to individuals. Its objectives are (1) to enlarge the supply of trained personnel for the rehabilitation of physically or mentally handicapped persons; (2) to improve the knowledge and skills of personnel already engaged in rehabilitation services; and (3) to instill a better understanding of rehabilitation philosophy and process on the part of all students enrolled in basic professional training programs preparing personnel for work in rehabilitation services. Rehabilitation research fellowships at the predoctoral and postdoctoral level are awarded to competent research workers in the professional fields which contribute to the vocational rehabilitation of disabled persons.

The Vocational Rehabilitation Ad ministration makes grants to public and other nonprofit organizations and agencies for paying part of the cost of projects for research and demonstrations, and projects for the establish-

ment of special facilities and services which hold promise of making a substantial contribution to the solution of vocational rehabilitation problems common to all or several States. Special project grants are made upon review and recommendation of a National Advisory Council on Vocational Rehabilitation. 

The Administration cooperates with the Bureau of Employees' Compensation, Department of Labor, in procuring rehabilitation services for Federal employees from State vocational rehabilitation agencies pursuant to the vocational rehabilitation provisions of the Federal Employees' Compensation

Act Amendments of 1949 (63 Stat. 

854-868; 5 U.S.C. 752-796).

The Vocational Rehabilitation Ad ministration is also responsible for research, research training, the interchange of rehabilitation experts, and other special rehabilitation activities overseas under the Foreign Currency

Program (section 104(k) of the Agri cultural Trade Development and As sistance Act of 1954, as amended, 72 

Stat. 275; 7 U.S.C. 1704, and section 4 of the International Health Research 

Act of 1960, 74 Stat. 365; 22 U.S.C. 

2102). These activities are designed to: (1) lead to the development of new knowledge and techniques for eliminating or reducing the handicapping effects of disability or (2) provide new application of existing knowledge and techniques to rehabilitation problems.

Research projects are expected to be of mutual benefit to rehabilitation in the United States and in the country in which the project is carried out. 

The Vocational Rehabilitation Ad ministration also plans and develops training programs in rehabilitation suited to the needs of nationals of other countries. These activities are carried out in cooperation with the United Nations and its specialized agencies, the Agency for International 

Development, the Department of

State, and numerous voluntary organizations. 

Food and Drug Administration 

Regulations, Title 21, Chapter I] CREATION AND AUTHORITY.- -The name "Food and Drug Administration" was first provided by the Agricultural Appropriation Act of 1931, approved May 27, 1930 (46 Stat. 392), although similar law-enforcement functions had been carried on under different organizational titles since 

January 1, 1907, when the Food and 

Drugs Act of 1906 (34 Stat. 768; 21 

U.S.C. 1-15) became effective. For a more complete history of the Food and 

Drug Administration, see appendix A.

PURPOSE.-The Food and Drug 

Administration administers the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act,

Tea Importation Act, Import Milk 

Act, Caustic Poison Act, Hazardous

Substances Labeling Act, and Filled 

Milk Act. Its activities are directed mainly toward promoting purity, standard potency, and truthful and informative labeling of consumer products covered by this legislation. 

ORGANIZATION.-The Food and 

Drug Administration operates under the direction of the Commissioner of 

Food and Drugs, who is responsible to the Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare. Its Washington headquarters consist of executive, professional, and service staffs located in the 

Office of the Commissioner and five

Bureaus which specialize in scientific research and analysis, medical evaluation, and regulatory and voluntary compliance. To provide nationwide coverage, the United States is divided into 18 district territories, each with headquarters manned by chemists and

KRA

inspectors and fully equipped with testing laboratories. Within these dis- 

El trict territories are 46 inspection stations located closer to industrial concentrations than district headquarters offices to expedite consumer i protection. 

REGULATORY OPERATIONS.-Each field district is responsible for maintaining surveillance over practices regulated by the six basic laws. Factories are inspected for sanitary conditions, raw materials used, and controls exercised in compounding, processing, packaging, and labeling products destined for interstate shipment. When violations are suspected, shipments are reported for destination sampling as a basis for regulatory action. Each district also keeps under surveillance imports offered for entry at its ports, on which are refused admission into the 

United States if they do not comply with applicable laws. Retail drugstores are kept under surveillance to prevent the dispensing of dangerous drugs without prescription.

Slu The regulatory program is developed on a selective project basis, with primary attention accorded to violations most serious to the public welfare, and, so far as practicable, with simultaneous and uniform nationwide action. When domestic violations are found, the facts are reported to the Department of Justice with a recommendation for seizure, criminal prosecution, or injunction actions in the 

Federal courts.

EDUCATION AND VOLUNTARY COM- 

PLIANCE.-Mass media and individual communications, oral and written, are used to promote better understanding and cooperation by consumers and industry. This includes assistance to manufacturers who request it, through comments on labeling, and suggestions concerning changes in manufacturing procedures, improvements in sanitary controls, and other methods to bring about compliance with legal requirements. Various means are used to advise consumers of the intent of the 

FDA programs, what they should expect of FDA, and how they can protect themselves. 

SCIENTIFIC INVESTIGATIONS.-The 

Washington laboratories (in addition to testing samples that requires specialized techniques and laboratory facilities not available at field laboratories) conduct fundamental research to determine characteristics of consumer products and production techniques, establish standards and tolerances for consumer protection, and develop methods capable of demonstrating violations in court actions. 

These investigations encompass the evaluation of the safety and efficacy of medicines; the toxicity of ingredients used in the manufacture of foods, drugs, and cosmetics; the safety of pesticidal and radioactive residues on food crops; the normal composition of all products covered by the acts admini̇stered; the potency of drugs and vitamins; and methods of processing, packaging, preserving, and storing products under adequate controls.

CONTROL OF NEW OR INVESTIGA- 

TIONAL DRUGS.—Applications for distributing new drugs (accompanied by the manufacturers' evidence establishing safety and effectiveness for use and adequacy of manufacturing controls) are evaluated and must be approved before each new drug is placed upon the market. The Kefauver-Harris

Drug Amendments of 1962 provide stronger controls of new drugs during their investigational stage and after marketing is approved, and a greater degree of safety and reliability of prescription drugs.

FOOD STANDARDS.-Intensive studies are made of composition, trade practices, and consumer understanding as a basis for formulating definitions and standards for foods that will promote honesty and fair dealing in the interest of the consumer. 

FOOD ADDITIVES AND PESTICIDE TOL- 

ERANCES.-No new additive may be

used in or on food until the promoter submits convincing evidence of its safety when tested on animals. If such evidence clearly demonstrates that the component is safe and will not deceive the consumer, regulations are issued specifying how it may be used. 

When shipped, no pesticide residue may remain on a raw agricultural commodity that exceeds an established tolerance after review of the promoter's scientific tests proving its safety.

ANTIBIOTICS, COLORS, INSULIN CER

are re- 

TIFICATION.-Manufacturers quired to prove safety and/or efficacy.

Safe limits on the amounts which may be used are set. Certification of each batch, not exempt by regulation, is required prior to marketing.

HOUSEHOLD CHEMICALS.-Labeling of household chemical aids such as waxes, polishes, and cleaning agents must bear prominent labeling as to the type of hazard, how to avoid injury, and first-aid measures in case of accidental injury. Regulations are published specifying how labeling is to appear and on what products.

Saint Elizabeths Hospital 

Regulations, Title 42, Chapter III]  

Hospital was first established by act of 

March 3, 1855 (10 Stat. 682), as the

Government Hospital for the Insane. 

It became Saint Elizabeths Hospital by act of July 1, 1916 (39 Stat. 309; 24

PURPOSE. The statutory mission of 

Saint Elizabeths Hospital is to provide "the most humane care and enlightened curative treatment" to the mentally ill.

ACTIVITIES.-The activities of Saint 

Elizabeths Hospital are divided among three major areas: 

1. Treatment.-This involves the therapeutic, rehabilitative, and protective programs for an average of more than 7,000 patients including residents of the District of Columbia, beneficiaries of the Veterans Administration, beneficiaries of the Public Health Serv ice, mentally ill persons charged with or convicted of crimes in U.S. courts including the courts of the District of

Columbia, certain American citizens and nationals found mentally ill in foreign countries, the Canal Zone, and the Virgin Islands, and members of the military services admitted to the Hospital prior to July 16, 1946. 

2. Training and Education.-The training and education program provides multidisciplinary clinical training for professional and other personnel engaged or interested in mental health activities. 

3. Research.-The Hospital plans, develops, and carries out coordinated research programs and projects for the purpose of obtaining a better understanding of the causes of mental disorders, and of the factors bearing upon their development, treatment, and possible prevention. A close working relationship is maintained with the Na tional Institute of Mental Health.
